364. Special provisions as to major ports and aerodromes.—(1) 
Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, the President may by public 
notification direct that as from such date as may be specified in the 
notification— 
(a) any law made by Parliament or by the Legislature of a State 
shall not apply to any major port or aerodrome or shall apply thereto 
subject to such exceptions or modifications as may be specified in the 
notification; or 
(b) any existing law shall cease to have effect in any major port or 
aerodrome except as respects things done or omitted to be done before 
the said date, or shall in its application to such port or aerodrome have 
effect subject to such exceptions or modifications as may be specified in 
the notification.
(2) In this article—
(a) “major port” means a port declared to be a major port by or 
under any law made by Parliament or any existing law and includes all 
areas for the time being included within the limits of such port;
(b) “aerodrome” means aerodrome as defined for the purposes of 
the enactments relating to airways, aircraft and air navigation.
365. Effect of failure to comply with, or to give effect to, directions 
given by the Union.—Where any State has failed to comply with, or to give 
effect to, any directions given in the exercise of the executive power of the Union 
under any of the provisions of this Constitution, it shall be lawful for the 
President to hold that a situation has arisen in which the Government of the State 
cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of this Constitution.
366. Definitions.—In this Constitution, unless the context otherwise 
requires, the following expressions have the meanings hereby respectively 
assigned to them, that is to say—
(1) “agricultural income” means agricultural income as defined 
for the purposes of the enactments relating to Indian income-tax;

descent but who is domiciled within the territory of India and is or was

established there for temporary purposes only;
(3) “article” means an article of this Constitution;

annuities, and “loan” shall be construed accordingly;

(b) that no deduction in respect of the tax paid by

authorised to be made from dividends payable by the companies

(c) that no provision exists for taking the tax so paid into

AMENDMENT OF THE CONSTITUTION
368. 
1[Power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and

Parliament may in exercise of its constituent power amend by way of addition, 
variation or repeal any provision of this Constitution in accordance with the 
procedure laid down in this article.] 
3[(2)] An amendment of this Constitution may be initiated only by the 
introduction of a Bill for the purpose in either House of Parliament, and when 
the Bill is passed in each House by a majority of the total membership of that 
House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that 
House present and voting, 4[it shall be presented to the President who shall give 
his assent to the Bill and thereupon] the Constitution shall stand amended in 
accordance with the terms of the Bill:

369. Temporary power to Parliament to make laws with respect to 
certain matters in the State List as if they were matters in the Concurrent

a period of five years from the commencement of this Constitution, have power

in the Concurrent List, namely:—

and distribution of, cotton and woollen textiles, raw cotton (including 
ginned cotton and unginned cotton or kapas), cotton seed, paper 
(including newsprint), food-stuffs (including edible oilseeds and oil), 
cattle fodder (including oil-cakes and other concentrates), coal 
(including coke and derivatives of coal), iron, steel and mica;

in clause (a), jurisdiction and powers of all courts except the Supreme 
Court with respect to any of those matters, and fees in respect of any of 
those matters but not including fees taken in any court,
but any law made by Parliament, which Parliament would not but for the 
provisions of this article have been competent to make, shall, to the extent of the 
incompetency, cease to have effect on the expiration of the said period, except as 
respects things done or omitted to be done before the expiration thereof.

Explanation I.—The expression “law in force” in this article shall 
include a law passed or made by a Legislature or other competent authority in 
the territory of India before the commencement of this Constitution and not 
previously repealed, notwithstanding that it or parts of it may not be then in 
operation either at all or in particular areas.
Explanation II.—Any law passed or made by a Legislature or other 
competent authority in the territory of India which immediately before the 
commencement of this Constitution had extra-territorial effect as well as effect 
in the territory of India shall, subject to any such adaptations and modifications 
as aforesaid, continue to have such extra-territorial effect.
Explanation III.—Nothing in this article shall be construed as continuing 
any temporary law in force beyond the date fixed for its expiration or the date 
on which it would have expired if this Constitution had  not come into force.
Explanation IV.—An Ordinance promulgated by the Governor of a 
Province under section 88 of the Government of India Act, 1935, and in force 
immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall, unless 
withdrawn by the Governor of the corresponding State earlier, cease to operate 
at the expiration of six weeks from the first meeting after such commencement 
of the Legislative Assembly of that State functioning under clause (1) of article 
382, and  nothing in this article shall be construed as continuing any such 
Ordinance in force beyond the said period.
1[372A.  Power of the President to adapt laws.—(1) For the purposes 
of bringing the provisions of any law in force in India or in any part thereof, 
immediately before the commencement of the Constitution (Seventh

amended by that Act, the President may by order made before the first day of 
November, 1957, make such adaptations and modifications of the law, whether 
by way of repeal or amendment, as may be necessary or expedient, and provide 
that the law shall, as from such date as may be  specified in the order, have 
effect subject to the adaptations and modifications so made, and any such 
adaptation or modification shall not be questioned in any court of law.
(2) Nothing in clause (1) shall be deemed to  prevent a competent 
Legislature or other competent authority from repealing or amending any law

373. Power of President to make order in respect of persons under 
preventive detention in certain cases.—Until provision is made by Parliament 
under clause (7) of article 22, or until the expiration of one year from the 
commencement of this Constitution, whichever  is earlier, the said  article shall 
have effect as if for any reference to Parliament in clauses (4) and (7) thereof 
there were substituted a reference to the President and for any reference to any 
law made by Parliament in those clauses there were substituted a reference to 
an order made by the President.
374. Provisions as to Judges of the Federal Court and proceedings 
pending in the Federal Court or before His Majesty in Council.—(1) The 
Judges of the Federal Court holding office immediately before the 
commencement of this Constitution shall, unless they have elected otherwise, 
become on such commencement the Judges of the Supreme Court and shall 
thereupon be entitled to such salaries and allowances and to such rights in 
respect of leave of absence and pension as are provided for under article 125 in 
respect of the Judges of the Supreme Court.
(2) All suits, appeals and proceedings, civil or criminal, pending in the 
Federal Court at the commencement of this Constitution shall stand removed to 
the Supreme Court, and the Supreme Court shall have jurisdiction to hear and 
determine the same, and the judgments and  orders of the Federal Court delivered 
or made before the  commencement of this Constitution shall have the same force 
and effect as if they had been delivered or made by the Supreme Court.
(3) Nothing in this Constitution shall operate to invalidate the exercise of 
jurisdiction by His Majesty in Council to dispose of appeals and petitions from, 
or in respect of, any judgment, decree or order of any court within the territory 
of India in so far as the exercise of such jurisdiction is authorised by law, and 
any order of His Majesty in Council made on any such appeal or petition after 
the commencement of this Constitution shall for all purposes have effect as if it 
were an order or decree made by the Supreme Court in the exercise of the  
jurisdiction conferred on such Court by this Constitution.
(4) On and from the commencement of this Constitution the jurisdiction of 
the authority functioning as the Privy Council in a State specified in Part B of the 
First Schedule to entertain and dispose of appeals and petitions from or in respect 
of any judgment, decree or order of any court within that State shall cease, and all 
appeals and other proceedings pending before the said authority at such 
commencement shall be transferred to, and disposed of by, the Supreme Court.
(5) Further provision may be made by Parliament by law to give effect to 
the provisions of this article.

375. Courts, authorities and officers to continue to function subject 
to the provisions of the Constitution.—All courts of civil, criminal and 
revenue jurisdiction, all authorities and all officers, judicial, executive and 
ministerial, throughout the territory of India, shall continue to exercise their 
respective functions subject to the provisions of this Constitution.
376. Provisions as to Judges of High Courts.—(1) Notwithstanding 
anything in clause (2) of article 217, the Judges of a High Court in any 
Province holding office immediately before the commencement of this 
Constitution shall, unless they have elected otherwise, become on such 
commencement the Judges of the High Court in the corresponding State, and 
shall thereupon be entitled to such salaries and allowances and to such rights in  
respect of leave of absence and pension as are provided for under article 221 in 
respect of the Judges of such High Court. 1[Any such Judge shall, 
notwithstanding that he is not a citizen of India, be eligible for appointment as 
Chief Justice of such High Court, or as Chief Justice or other Judge of any 
other High Court.] 
(2) The Judges of a High Court in any Indian State corresponding to any 
State specified in Part B of the First Schedule holding office immediately 
before the commencement of this Constitution shall, unless they have elected 
otherwise, become on such commencement the Judges of the High Court in the 
State so specified and shall, notwithstanding anything in clauses  (1) and (2) of 
article 217 but subject to the proviso to clause (1) of that article, continue to hold 
office until the expiration of such period as the President may by order determine. 
(3)  In this article, the expression “Judge” does not include an acting Judge 
or an additional Judge.
377. Provisions as to Comptroller and Auditor-General of India.—The 
Auditor-General of India holding office immediately before the commencement of 
this Constitution shall, unless  he has elected otherwise, become on such 
commencement the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India and shall thereupon 
be entitled to such salaries and to such rights in respect of leave of absence and 
pension as are provided for under clause (3) of article 148 in respect of the 
Comptroller and Auditor-General of India and be entitled to continue to hold office 
until the expiration of his term of office as determined under the provisions which 
were applicable to him immediately before such commencement.

PART XXII
SHORT TITLE, COMMENCEMENT, 1[AUTHORITATIVE 
TEXT IN HINDI] AND REPEALS
393. Short title.—This Constitution may be called the Constitution of 
India. 
394.  Commencement.—This article and articles 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60,  324, 
366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392 and 393 shall come into force at once, and 
the remaining provisions of this Constitution shall come into force on the 
twenty-sixth day of January, 1950, which day is referred to in this Constitution 
as the commencement of this Constitution. 
2[394A. Authoritative text in the Hindi language.—(1) The President 
shall cause to be published under his authority,— 
(a) the translation of this Constitution in the Hindi language, 
signed by the members of the Constituent Assembly, with such 
modifications as may be necessary to bring it in conformity with the 
language, style and terminology adopted in the authoritative texts of 
Central Acts in the Hindi language, and incorporating therein all the 
amendments of this Constitution made before such publication; and
(b) the translation in the Hindi language of every amendment of 
this Constitution made in the English language. 
(2) The translation of this Constitution and of every amendment thereof 
published under clause (1) shall be construed to have the same meaning as  the 
original thereof and if any difficulty arises in so construing any part of such 
translation, the President shall cause the same to be revised suitably.
(3) The translation of this Constitution and of every amendment thereof 
published under this article shall  be deemed to be, for all purposes, the 
authoritative text thereof in the Hindi language.]
395. Repeals.—
The Indian Independence Act, 1947, and the 
Government of India Act, 1935, together with all enactments amending or 
supplementing the latter Act, but not including the Abolition of Privy Council 
Jurisdiction Act, 1949, are hereby repealed.

nodes.summary: The partial document outlines specific provisions from the Constitution of India, particularly focusing on miscellaneous articles. It discusses the abolition of the privy purse as per the Twenty-sixth Amendment Act of 1971, extinguishing all rights related to it for former rulers. It also details the President's authority to modify the application of laws concerning major ports and aerodromes, including the definitions of these terms. Additionally, it addresses the consequences of a state's failure to comply with directions from the Union, allowing the President to determine if the state government can function according to constitutional provisions. Lastly, it provides a definition of "agricultural income" as it pertains to Indian income tax laws.

Ruler, referred to in clause (a) or any other person shall not be paid any

364. Special provisions as to major ports and aerodromes.—(1) 
Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, the President may by public 
notification direct that as from such date as may be specified in the 
notification— 
(a) any law made by Parliament or by the Legislature of a State 
shall not apply to any major port or aerodrome or shall apply thereto 
subject to such exceptions or modifications as may be specified in the 
notification; or 
(b) any existing law shall cease to have effect in any major port or 
aerodrome except as respects things done or omitted to be done before 
the said date, or shall in its application to such port or aerodrome have 
effect subject to such exceptions or modifications as may be specified in 
the notification.
(2) In this article—
(a) “major port” means a port declared to be a major port by or 
under any law made by Parliament or any existing law and includes all 
areas for the time being included within the limits of such port;
(b) “aerodrome” means aerodrome as defined for the purposes of 
the enactments relating to airways, aircraft and air navigation.
365. Effect of failure to comply with, or to give effect to, directions 
given by the Union.—Where any State has failed to comply with, or to give 
effect to, any directions given in the exercise of the executive power of the Union 
under any of the provisions of this Constitution, it shall be lawful for the 
President to hold that a situation has arisen in which the Government of the State 
cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of this Constitution.
366. Definitions.—In this Constitution, unless the context otherwise 
requires, the following expressions have the meanings hereby respectively 
assigned to them, that is to say—
(1) “agricultural income” means agricultural income as defined 
for the purposes of the enactments relating to Indian income-tax;

It discusses the abolition of the privy purse as per the Twenty-sixth Amendment Act of 1971, extinguishing all rights related to it. It also details the President's authority to modify the application of laws concerning major ports and aerodromes, including the definitions of these terms. AMENDMENT OF THE CONSTITUTION
Power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and procedure therefor.
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines the procedures and powers related to the amendment of the Constitution of India, specifically under Article 368. It details the process by which Parliament can initiate amendments, requiring a Bill to be passed by a majority in both Houses and subsequently receiving the President's assent. Certain amendments, particularly those affecting specific articles and provisions, necessitate ratification by at least half of the State Legislatures. The document also clarifies that amendments cannot be challenged in court and asserts that there are no limitations on Parliament's power to amend the Constitution. Additionally, it includes provisions for temporary, transitional, and special arrangements for various states, such as Jammu and Kashmir, Nagaland, and others, highlighting the unique governance and legislative powers granted to these regions. The document emphasizes the President's role in facilitating adaptations of laws and the establishment of special responsibilities for governors in certain states.

by a competent Legislature or other competent authority.

territory of India into accord with the provisions of this Constitution, the

whether by way of repeal or amendment, as may be necessary or expedient, and 
provide that the law shall, as from such date as may be specified in the order, 
have effect subject to the adaptations and modifications so made, and any such 
adaptation or modification shall not be questioned in any court of law.

373. Power of President to make order in respect of persons under 
preventive detention in certain cases.—Until provision is made by Parliament 
under clause (7) of article 22, or until the expiration of one year from the 
commencement of this Constitution, whichever  is earlier, the said  article shall 
have effect as if for any reference to Parliament in clauses (4) and (7) thereof 
there were substituted a reference to the President and for any reference to any 
law made by Parliament in those clauses there were substituted a reference to 
an order made by the President.
374. Provisions as to Judges of the Federal Court and proceedings 
pending in the Federal Court or before His Majesty in Council.—(1) The 
Judges of the Federal Court holding office immediately before the 
commencement of this Constitution shall, unless they have elected otherwise, 
become on such commencement the Judges of the Supreme Court and shall 
thereupon be entitled to such salaries and allowances and to such rights in 
respect of leave of absence and pension as are provided for under article 125 in 
respect of the Judges of the Supreme Court.
(2) All suits, appeals and proceedings, civil or criminal, pending in the 
Federal Court at the commencement of this Constitution shall stand removed to 
the Supreme Court, and the Supreme Court shall have jurisdiction to hear and 
determine the same, and the judgments and  orders of the Federal Court delivered 
or made before the  commencement of this Constitution shall have the same force 
and effect as if they had been delivered or made by the Supreme Court.
(3) Nothing in this Constitution shall operate to invalidate the exercise of 
jurisdiction by His Majesty in Council to dispose of appeals and petitions from, 
or in respect of, any judgment, decree or order of any court within the territory 
of India in so far as the exercise of such jurisdiction is authorised by law, and 
any order of His Majesty in Council made on any such appeal or petition after 
the commencement of this Constitution shall for all purposes have effect as if it 
were an order or decree made by the Supreme Court in the exercise of the  
jurisdiction conferred on such Court by this Constitution.
(4) On and from the commencement of this Constitution the jurisdiction of 
the authority functioning as the Privy Council in a State specified in Part B of the 
First Schedule to entertain and dispose of appeals and petitions from or in respect 
of any judgment, decree or order of any court within that State shall cease, and all 
appeals and other proceedings pending before the said authority at such 
commencement shall be transferred to, and disposed of by, the Supreme Court.
(5) Further provision may be made by Parliament by law to give effect to 
the provisions of this article.

369. Temporary power to Parliament to make laws with respect to 
certain matters in the State List as if they were matters in the Concurrent 
List.—Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament shall, during 
a period of five years from the commencement of this Constitution, have power 
to make laws with respect to the following matters as if they were enumerated 
in the Concurrent List, namely:— 
(a) trade and commerce within a State in, and the production, supply 
and distribution of, cotton and woollen textiles, raw cotton (including 
ginned cotton and unginned cotton or kapas), cotton seed, paper 
(including newsprint), food-stuffs (including edible oilseeds and oil), 
cattle fodder (including oil-cakes and other concentrates), coal 
(including coke and derivatives of coal), iron, steel and mica;
(b) offences against laws with respect to any of the matters mentioned
in clause (a), jurisdiction and powers of all courts except the Supreme 
Court with respect to any of those matters, and fees in respect of any of 
those matters but not including fees taken in any court,
but any law made by Parliament, which Parliament would not but for the 
provisions of this article have been competent to make, shall, to the extent of the 
incompetency, cease to have effect on the expiration of the said period, except as 
respects things done or omitted to be done before the expiration thereof.

there were substituted a reference to the President and for any reference to any 
law made by Parliament in those clauses there were substituted a reference to 
an order made by the President.
374. Provisions as to Judges of the Federal Court and proceedings 
pending in the Federal Court or before His Majesty in Council.—(1) The 
Judges of the Federal Court holding office immediately before the 
commencement of this Constitution shall, unless they have elected otherwise, 
become on such commencement the Judges of the Supreme Court and shall 
thereupon be entitled to such salaries and allowances and to such rights in 
respect of leave of absence and pension as are provided for under article 125 in 
respect of the Judges of the Supreme Court.
(2) All suits, appeals and proceedings, civil or criminal, pending in the 
Federal Court at the commencement of this Constitution shall stand removed to 
the Supreme Court, and the Supreme Court shall have jurisdiction to hear and 
determine the same, and the judgments and  orders of the Federal Court delivered 
or made before the  commencement of this Constitution shall have the same force 
and effect as if they had been delivered or made by the Supreme Court.
(3) Nothing in this Constitution shall operate to invalidate the exercise of 
jurisdiction by His Majesty in Council to dispose of appeals and petitions from, 
or in respect of, any judgment, decree or order of any court within the territory 
of India in so far as the exercise of such jurisdiction is authorised by law, and 
any order of His Majesty in Council made on any such appeal or petition after 
the commencement of this Constitution shall for all purposes have effect as if it 
were an order or decree made by the Supreme Court in the exercise of the  
jurisdiction conferred on such Court by this Constitution.
(4) On and from the commencement of this Constitution the jurisdiction of 
the authority functioning as the Privy Council in a State specified in Part B of the 
First Schedule to entertain and dispose of appeals and petitions from or in respect 
of any judgment, decree or order of any court within that State shall cease, and all 
appeals and other proceedings pending before the said authority at such 
commencement shall be transferred to, and disposed of by, the Supreme Court.
(5) Further provision may be made by Parliament by law to give effect to 
the provisions of this article.

nodes.summary: The partial document outlines the procedure for amending the Constitution as specified in Article 368. It states that Parliament has the power to amend the Constitution through a Bill introduced in either House, which must be passed by a majority of the total membership and a two-thirds majority of those present and voting. The amendment must then receive the President's assent to take effect. Additionally, it specifies certain articles and provisions that require special consideration if amendments are proposed, indicating that changes to these areas involve more stringent requirements.

AMENDMENT OF THE CONSTITUTION
368. 
1[Power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and 
procedure therefor].— 2[(1) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, 
Parliament may in exercise of its constituent power amend by way of addition, 
variation or repeal any provision of this Constitution in accordance with the 
procedure laid down in this article.] 
3[(2)] An amendment of this Constitution may be initiated only by the 
introduction of a Bill for the purpose in either House of Parliament, and when 
the Bill is passed in each House by a majority of the total membership of that 
House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that 
House present and voting, 4[it shall be presented to the President who shall give 
his assent to the Bill and thereupon] the Constitution shall stand amended in 
accordance with the terms of the Bill:

TEMPORARY, TRANSITIONAL AND SPECIAL PROVISIONS
Temporary power to Parliament to make laws with respect to certain matters in the State List as if they were matters in the Concurrent List.
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines temporary and transitional provisions in the Constitution of India, specifically focusing on the powers of Parliament regarding certain matters in the State List and special provisions related to the State of Jammu and Kashmir. It details the temporary authority granted to Parliament to legislate on specific subjects as if they were in the Concurrent List for a period of five years from the Constitution's commencement. These subjects include trade, commerce, and various commodities. Additionally, it discusses the limitations on Parliament's power to legislate for Jammu and Kashmir, emphasizing the need for consultation with the State Government and referencing the Instrument of Accession. The document also notes the cessation of certain clauses of Article 370, which previously granted special status to Jammu and Kashmir, and outlines the application of the Constitution to the State without modifications or exceptions.

PART XXI
1[TEMPORARY, TRANSITIONAL AND 
SPECIAL PROVISIONS] 
369. Temporary power to Parliament to make laws with respect to 
certain matters in the State List as if they were matters in the Concurrent 
List.—Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament shall, during 
a period of five years from the commencement of this Constitution, have power 
to make laws with respect to the following matters as if they were enumerated 
in the Concurrent List, namely:— 
(a) trade and commerce within a State in, and the production, supply 
and distribution of, cotton and woollen textiles, raw cotton (including 
ginned cotton and unginned cotton or kapas), cotton seed, paper 
(including newsprint), food-stuffs (including edible oilseeds and oil), 
cattle fodder (including oil-cakes and other concentrates), coal 
(including coke and derivatives of coal), iron, steel and mica;
(b) offences against laws with respect to any of the matters mentioned
in clause (a), jurisdiction and powers of all courts except the Supreme 
Court with respect to any of those matters, and fees in respect of any of 
those matters but not including fees taken in any court,
but any law made by Parliament, which Parliament would not but for the 
provisions of this article have been competent to make, shall, to the extent of the 
incompetency, cease to have effect on the expiration of the said period, except as 
respects things done or omitted to be done before the expiration thereof.
______________________________________________

AND TRANSITIONAL PROVISIONS" (w.e.f. 1-12-1963).

nodes.summary: The partial document outlines special provisions in the Constitution of India concerning the states of Maharashtra, Gujarat, and Nagaland. Additionally, it specifies that certain laws related to religious practices, customary law, and land ownership in Nagaland will not apply unless the state's Legislative Assembly decides otherwise. nodes.title: Special provision with respect to the State of Nagaland.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines special provisions in the Constitution of India concerning various states, particularly focusing on Maharashtra, Gujarat, Nagaland, Assam, Manipur, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Sikkim, Mizoram, and Arunachal Pradesh. Key points include:

1. **Maharashtra and Gujarat**: The President can assign special responsibilities to the Governors for establishing development boards, equitable fund allocation, and ensuring technical education and employment opportunities in specific regions.

2. **Nagaland**: The document specifies that certain parliamentary acts do not apply unless the Nagaland Legislative Assembly decides otherwise. It also grants the Governor special responsibilities regarding law and order and the administration of the Tuensang district, including the establishment of a regional council.

3. **Assam and Manipur**: Provisions for the constitution and functions of committees within the Legislative Assemblies to represent tribal areas and hill regions, respectively, are outlined, along with the Governor's responsibilities in these matters.

4. **Andhra Pradesh and Telangana**: The President can create orders for equitable opportunities in public employment and education, and establish an Administrative Tribunal to oversee civil service matters.

5. **Sikkim**: The document details the formation of the Legislative Assembly, representation in the House of the People, and the Governor's responsibilities for social and economic advancement.

6. **Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh**: Special provisions regarding the application of parliamentary acts related to local customs and laws, as well as the Governor's responsibilities for law and order, are highlighted.

Overall, the document emphasizes the unique administrative and legislative frameworks established for these states to address their specific social, cultural, and developmental needs.

(b) the Governor of Nagaland shall have special responsibility with 
respect to law and order in the State of Nagaland for so long as in his 
opinion internal disturbances occurring in the Naga Hills-Tuensang Area 
immediately before the formation of that State continue therein  or in any 
part thereof and in the discharge of his functions in relation thereto the 
Governor shall, after consulting the Council of Ministers, exercise his 
individual judgment as to the action to be taken:
Provided that if any question  arises whether any matter is or is 
not a matter as respects which the Governor is under  this sub-clause 
required to act in the exercise of his individual judgment, the decision of 
the Governor in  his discretion shall be  final, and the validity of 
anything done by the Governor shall not be called in question on the 
ground that he ought or ought not to have acted in the exercise of his 
individual judgment: 
Provided further that if the President on receipt  of a report from 
the Governor or otherwise is satisfied that it is no longer necessary for 
the Governor to have special responsibility with respect to law and order 
in the State of Nagaland, he may by order direct that the Governor shall 
cease to have such responsibility with effect from such date as may be 
specified in the order;
(c) in making his recommendation with respect to any demand for a 
grant, the Governor of Nagaland shall ensure that any money provided 
by the Government of India out of the Consolidated Fund of  India for 
any specific service or purpose is included in the demand for a grant 
relating to that service or purpose and not in any other demand;
(d) as from such date as the Governor of Nagaland may by public 
notification in this behalf specify, there shall be established a regional 
council for the Tuensang district consisting  of thirty-five members and 
the Governor shall in his discretion make rules providing for—
(i) the composition of the regional council and the manner in 
which the members of the regional council shall be chosen:
Provided that the Deputy Commissioner of the Tuensang district  
shall be the Chairman ex officio of the regional council and the Vice-
Chairman of the regional council shall be elected by the members 
thereof from amongst themselves;
(ii) the qualifications for being chosen as, and for being, 
members of the regional council;
(iii) the term of office of, and the salaries and allowances, if any, 
to be paid to members of, the regional council;

(iv) the procedure and conduct of business of the regional council;
(v) the appointment  of officers and staff of the regional council 
and their conditions of services; and
(vi) any other matter in respect of which it is necessary to make 
rules for the constitution and proper functioning of the regional council.
(2) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, for a period of ten 
years from the date of the formation of the State of Nagaland or for such further 
period as the Governor may, on the recommendation of the regional council, by 
public notification specify in this behalf,—
(a) the administration of the Tuensang district shall be carried on by 
the Governor;
(b) where any money is provided by the Government of India to the 
Government of Nagaland to meet the requirements of the State of 
Nagaland as a whole, the Governor shall in his discretion arrange for an 
equitable allocation of that money between the Tuensang district and the 
rest of the State;

district unless the Governor, on the recommendation of the regional 
council, by public notification so directs and the Governor in giving such 
direction with respect to any such Act may direct that the Act shall in its 
application to the Tuensang district or any part thereof have effect 
subject to such exceptions or modifications as the Governor may specify 
on the recommendation of the regional council:
Provided that any direction given under this sub-clause may be 
given so as to have retrospective effect;
(d) the Governor may make regulations for the peace, progress and good 
government of the Tuensang district and any regulations so made may repeal 
or amend with retrospective effect, if necessary, any Act of Parliament or any 
other law which is for the time being applicable to that district;

Legislative Assembly of Nagaland shall be appointed Minister for 
Tuensang affairs by the Governor on the advice of the Chief Minister 
and the Chief Minister in tendering his advice shall act on the 
recommendation of the majority of the members as aforesaid1;

nodes.title: Special provision with respect to the State of Arunachal Pradesh.
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines specific provisions in the Constitution of India related to temporary, transitional, and special arrangements for certain states. It includes details about the validity of actions taken in Sikkim prior to the Constitution (Thirty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1975. It also specifies special provisions for the states of Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, and Karnataka. For Mizoram, it states that certain parliamentary acts do not apply unless the state assembly decides otherwise, and it mandates a minimum number of assembly members. Arunachal Pradesh's provisions grant the Governor special responsibilities regarding law and order, with the Governor's discretion being final in related matters. Goa's provision establishes a minimum assembly size, while Karnataka's provisions allow the President to assign special responsibilities to the Governor for regional development, including the establishment of a development board and equitable opportunities for residents.

Additionally, it details special provisions for Karnataka, including the establishment of a development board for the Hyderabad-Karnataka region, equitable allocation of funds, and opportunities for local residents in education and employment, including potential reservations in educational institutions. The document references amendments that introduced these provisions.

nodes.title: Special provisions with respect to State of Karnataka.
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines specific provisions of the Constitution of India related to temporary, transitional, and special arrangements. It discusses the powers and responsibilities of Governors in certain states, particularly Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, and Karnataka, including the establishment of development boards and equitable allocation of resources. The document also addresses the continuity of existing laws and their adaptation to align with the new Constitution, detailing the President's authority to modify laws and the transition of judicial roles from the Federal Court to the Supreme Court. Additionally, it covers the status of judges, public service commissions, and the provisions for the Legislative Assembly of Andhra Pradesh. The document concludes with articles regarding the short title, commencement, and authoritative text of the Constitution, as well as the repeal of previous acts.

372. Continuance in force of existing laws and their adaptation.—(1) 
Notwithstanding the repeal by this Constitution of the enactments referred to in 
article 395 but subject to the other provisions of this Constitution, all the law in 
force in the territory of India immediately before the commencement of this 
Constitution shall continue in force therein until altered or repealed or amended 
by a competent Legislature or other competent authority.
(2) For the purpose of bringing the provisions of any law in force in the 
territory of India into accord with the provisions of this Constitution, the 
President may by order make such adaptations and modifications of such law, 
whether by way of repeal or amendment, as may be necessary or expedient, and 
provide that the law shall, as from such date as may be specified in the order, 
have effect subject to the adaptations and modifications so made, and any such 
adaptation or modification shall not be questioned in any court of law.

modification of any law after the expiration of 1[three years] from the 
commencement of this Constitution; or

authority from repealing or amending any law adapted or modified by 
the President under the said clause.

(w.e.f. 18-6-1951).

THE CONSTITUTION OF  INDIA
(Part XXI.—Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions)
247
Explanation I.—The expression “law in force” in this article shall 
include a law passed or made by a Legislature or other competent authority in 
the territory of India before the commencement of this Constitution and not 
previously repealed, notwithstanding that it or parts of it may not be then in 
operation either at all or in particular areas.
Explanation II.—Any law passed or made by a Legislature or other 
competent authority in the territory of India which immediately before the 
commencement of this Constitution had extra-territorial effect as well as effect 
in the territory of India shall, subject to any such adaptations and modifications 
as aforesaid, continue to have such extra-territorial effect.
Explanation III.—Nothing in this article shall be construed as continuing 
any temporary law in force beyond the date fixed for its expiration or the date 
on which it would have expired if this Constitution had  not come into force.
Explanation IV.—An Ordinance promulgated by the Governor of a 
Province under section 88 of the Government of India Act, 1935, and in force 
immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall, unless 
withdrawn by the Governor of the corresponding State earlier, cease to operate 
at the expiration of six weeks from the first meeting after such commencement 
of the Legislative Assembly of that State functioning under clause (1) of article 
382, and  nothing in this article shall be construed as continuing any such 
Ordinance in force beyond the said period.
1[372A.  Power of the President to adapt laws.—(1) For the purposes 
of bringing the provisions of any law in force in India or in any part thereof, 
immediately before the commencement of the Constitution (Seventh 
Amendment) Act, 1956, into accord with the provisions of this Constitution as 
amended by that Act, the President may by order made before the first day of 
November, 1957, make such adaptations and modifications of the law, whether 
by way of repeal or amendment, as may be necessary or expedient, and provide 
that the law shall, as from such date as may be  specified in the order, have 
effect subject to the adaptations and modifications so made, and any such 
adaptation or modification shall not be questioned in any court of law.
(2) Nothing in clause (1) shall be deemed to  prevent a competent 
Legislature or other competent authority from repealing or amending any law 
adapted or modified by the President  under the said clause.]
______________________________________________
1. Ins. by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, s. 23 (w.e.f. 1-11-1956).
 See the Adaptation of Laws Order of 1956 and 1957. 

THE CONSTITUTION OF  INDIA
(Part XXI.—Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions)
248
373. Power of President to make order in respect of persons under 
preventive detention in certain cases.—Until provision is made by Parliament 
under clause (7) of article 22, or until the expiration of one year from the 
commencement of this Constitution, whichever  is earlier, the said  article shall 
have effect as if for any reference to Parliament in clauses (4) and (7) thereof 
there were substituted a reference to the President and for any reference to any 
law made by Parliament in those clauses there were substituted a reference to 
an order made by the President.
374. Provisions as to Judges of the Federal Court and proceedings 
pending in the Federal Court or before His Majesty in Council.—(1) The 
Judges of the Federal Court holding office immediately before the 
commencement of this Constitution shall, unless they have elected otherwise, 
become on such commencement the Judges of the Supreme Court and shall 
thereupon be entitled to such salaries and allowances and to such rights in 
respect of leave of absence and pension as are provided for under article 125 in 
respect of the Judges of the Supreme Court.
(2) All suits, appeals and proceedings, civil or criminal, pending in the 
Federal Court at the commencement of this Constitution shall stand removed to 
the Supreme Court, and the Supreme Court shall have jurisdiction to hear and 
determine the same, and the judgments and  orders of the Federal Court delivered 
or made before the  commencement of this Constitution shall have the same force 
and effect as if they had been delivered or made by the Supreme Court.
(3) Nothing in this Constitution shall operate to invalidate the exercise of 
jurisdiction by His Majesty in Council to dispose of appeals and petitions from, 
or in respect of, any judgment, decree or order of any court within the territory 
of India in so far as the exercise of such jurisdiction is authorised by law, and 
any order of His Majesty in Council made on any such appeal or petition after 
the commencement of this Constitution shall for all purposes have effect as if it 
were an order or decree made by the Supreme Court in the exercise of the  
jurisdiction conferred on such Court by this Constitution.
(4) On and from the commencement of this Constitution the jurisdiction of 
the authority functioning as the Privy Council in a State specified in Part B of the 
First Schedule to entertain and dispose of appeals and petitions from or in respect 
of any judgment, decree or order of any court within that State shall cease, and all 
appeals and other proceedings pending before the said authority at such 
commencement shall be transferred to, and disposed of by, the Supreme Court.
(5) Further provision may be made by Parliament by law to give effect to 
the provisions of this article.

THE CONSTITUTION OF  INDIA
(Part XXI.—Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions)
249
375. Courts, authorities and officers to continue to function subject 
to the provisions of the Constitution.—All courts of civil, criminal and 
revenue jurisdiction, all authorities and all officers, judicial, executive and 
ministerial, throughout the territory of India, shall continue to exercise their 
respective functions subject to the provisions of this Constitution.
376. Provisions as to Judges of High Courts.—(1) Notwithstanding 
anything in clause (2) of article 217, the Judges of a High Court in any 
Province holding office immediately before the commencement of this 
Constitution shall, unless they have elected otherwise, become on such 
commencement the Judges of the High Court in the corresponding State, and 
shall thereupon be entitled to such salaries and allowances and to such rights in  
respect of leave of absence and pension as are provided for under article 221 in 
respect of the Judges of such High Court. 1[Any such Judge shall, 
notwithstanding that he is not a citizen of India, be eligible for appointment as 
Chief Justice of such High Court, or as Chief Justice or other Judge of any 
other High Court.] 
(2) The Judges of a High Court in any Indian State corresponding to any 
State specified in Part B of the First Schedule holding office immediately 
before the commencement of this Constitution shall, unless they have elected 
otherwise, become on such commencement the Judges of the High Court in the 
State so specified and shall, notwithstanding anything in clauses  (1) and (2) of 
article 217 but subject to the proviso to clause (1) of that article, continue to hold 
office until the expiration of such period as the President may by order determine. 
(3)  In this article, the expression “Judge” does not include an acting Judge 
or an additional Judge.
377. Provisions as to Comptroller and Auditor-General of India.—The 
Auditor-General of India holding office immediately before the commencement of 
this Constitution shall, unless  he has elected otherwise, become on such 
commencement the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India and shall thereupon 
be entitled to such salaries and to such rights in respect of leave of absence and 
pension as are provided for under clause (3) of article 148 in respect of the 
Comptroller and Auditor-General of India and be entitled to continue to hold office 
until the expiration of his term of office as determined under the provisions which 
were applicable to him immediately before such commencement.
______________________________________________
1. Added by the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951, s. 13 (w.e.f. 18-6-1951).

THE CONSTITUTION OF  INDIA
(Part XXI.—Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions)
250
378. Provisions as to Public Service Commissions.—(1) The members 
of the Public Service Commission for the Dominion of India holding office 
immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall, unless they 
have elected otherwise, become on such commencement the members of the 
Public Service Commission for the Union and shall, notwithstanding anything in

nodes.summary: The partial document outlines temporary provisions allowing the Parliament to legislate on specific matters typically reserved for the State List, treating them as if they were part of the Concurrent List for a period of five years from the Constitution's commencement. It specifies the areas of trade and commerce, production, and distribution of various goods, including textiles, foodstuffs, and minerals. Additionally, it addresses the jurisdiction of courts regarding these matters and stipulates that any laws made under this provision will cease to have effect after the five-year period, except for actions taken during that time.
nodes.text:

PART XXI
1[TEMPORARY, TRANSITIONAL AND 
SPECIAL PROVISIONS] 
369. Temporary power to Parliament to make laws with respect to 
certain matters in the State List as if they were matters in the Concurrent 
List.—Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament shall, during 
a period of five years from the commencement of this Constitution, have power 
to make laws with respect to the following matters as if they were enumerated 
in the Concurrent List, namely:— 
(a) trade and commerce within a State in, and the production, supply 
and distribution of, cotton and woollen textiles, raw cotton (including 
ginned cotton and unginned cotton or kapas), cotton seed, paper 
(including newsprint), food-stuffs (including edible oilseeds and oil), 
cattle fodder (including oil-cakes and other concentrates), coal 
(including coke and derivatives of coal), iron, steel and mica;
(b) offences against laws with respect to any of the matters mentioned
in clause (a), jurisdiction and powers of all courts except the Supreme 
Court with respect to any of those matters, and fees in respect of any of 
those matters but not including fees taken in any court,
but any law made by Parliament, which Parliament would not but for the 
provisions of this article have been competent to make, shall, to the extent of the 
incompetency, cease to have effect on the expiration of the said period, except as 
respects things done or omitted to be done before the expiration thereof.
______________________________________________
1. Subs. by the Constitution (Thirteenth Amendment) Act, 1962, s. 2, for  "TEMPORARY
AND TRANSITIONAL PROVISIONS" (w.e.f. 1-12-1963).

Short title.
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines key provisions related to the Constitution of India, including its short title, commencement, and the establishment of an authoritative Hindi text. It specifies that the Constitution may be referred to as the Constitution of India and details the articles that came into force immediately versus those that took effect on January 26, 1950. Additionally, it mandates the publication of a Hindi translation of the Constitution and its amendments, ensuring that this translation holds the same authoritative status as the original English text. Finally, the document repeals previous legislative acts, specifically the Indian Independence Act of 1947 and the Government of India Act of 1935, while excluding the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act of 1949.

It includes details about the formation of states such as Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand, Jharkhand, and Telangana, all of which were established through various reorganisation acts in the early 2000s and 2014. Additionally, it specifies the extent of union territories, including Delhi and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, as they were constituted prior to the commencement of the Constitution. The document also notes amendments and renumbering of entries related to these territories, reflecting changes made by subsequent legislative acts.

nodes.title: Telangana

It includes specific references to the reorganization acts that established states such as Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand, Jharkhand, and Telangana, along with their respective territories. Additionally, it lists union territories like Delhi, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, Puducherry, and Chandigarh, specifying their historical contexts and the legislative acts that defined their boundaries. The document also notes amendments and renumbering of entries related to these territories over time.

nodes.summary: The partial document outlines various forms of oaths or affirmations required for different officials in India, as specified in the Third Schedule of the Constitution. It includes the oath of office for Union Ministers, State Ministers, candidates for election to Parliament and State Legislatures, members of Parliament and State Legislatures, as well as judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts. Each oath emphasizes allegiance to the Constitution of India, the commitment to uphold the sovereignty and integrity of the nation, and the duty to perform their responsibilities without bias or favoritism. Additionally, the document includes a Fourth Schedule that details the allocation of seats in the Council of States for various states and Union territories, indicating the number of seats assigned to each.

nodes.title: FIFTH SCHEDULE
Provisions as to the Administration and Control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines the provisions related to the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in India, as specified in the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution. It includes several key points:

1. **Interpretation and Scope**: Defines "State" in the context of Scheduled Areas, excluding certain northeastern states.

2. **Executive Power**: States that the executive power of a State extends to Scheduled Areas, with the Governor required to report to the President on their administration.

3. **Tribes Advisory Council**: Establishes the requirement for a Tribes Advisory Council in states with Scheduled Areas, detailing its composition, duties, and the Governor's authority to regulate its functioning.

4. **Law Applicability**: Grants the Governor the power to exempt certain laws from applying to Scheduled Areas and to make regulations for governance, including land transfer and business practices among Scheduled Tribes.

5. **Scheduled Areas Definition**: Defines Scheduled Areas and outlines the President's authority to declare, modify, or rescind such areas.

6. **Amendment of the Schedule**: Allows Parliament to amend the provisions of the Schedule without it being considered a constitutional amendment.

Overall, the document emphasizes the governance framework for Scheduled Areas and the rights and protections for Scheduled Tribes, ensuring their welfare and advancement.

GENERAL

nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines provisions related to the governance of autonomous districts and regions in India as specified in the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution. Key points include:

1. **Governor's Authority**: The Governor can issue orders regarding the administration of autonomous districts after considering reports from a designated Commission.

2. **District and Regional Councils**: Each autonomous district will have a District Council with a maximum of thirty members, including elected representatives and those nominated by the Governor. Additionally, separate Regional Councils will be established for autonomous regions.

3. **Council Composition and Elections**: The document details the composition, election procedures, and qualifications for members of the District and Regional Councils, emphasizing adult suffrage and the role of the Governor in rule-making.

4. **Powers and Administration**: The District and Regional Councils are granted specific powers for local governance, including the ability to make rules and regulations concerning their administration and the conduct of business.

5. **Legislative Powers**: The Regional Councils have the authority to make laws on various subjects, including education, agriculture, and infrastructure, subject to the Governor's assent.

6. **Amendments and Provisions**: The document references several amendments that have modified the structure and powers of the councils, particularly in relation to specific regions like Assam.

Overall, the document emphasizes the framework for self-governance in tribal areas, detailing the roles, powers, and election processes of local councils.

nodes.title: Powers of the District Councils and Regional Councils to make laws.
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the provisions of the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution of India, which pertains to the governance and administration of autonomous regions and districts, particularly in the northeastern states. It outlines the powers of District Councils and Regional Councils to make laws on various subjects, including land use, agriculture, education, public health, and local governance. The document specifies the process for law-making, including the requirement for laws to be submitted to the Governor for assent and the role of the President in approving or returning laws for reconsideration. Additionally, it addresses the establishment of village councils or courts for administering justice within these autonomous areas, emphasizing the jurisdiction of these councils over disputes involving Scheduled Tribes. The text also notes amendments made to the provisions over time, reflecting changes in governance structures and responsibilities.

nodes.title: Administration of justice in autonomous districts and autonomous regions.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines provisions related to the administration of justice and governance in autonomous districts and regions under the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution of India. Key points include:

1. **Law Making and Governance**: Laws made by Regional and District Councils require the Governor's assent to take effect. Councils can establish village councils or courts for disputes involving Scheduled Tribes, with specific jurisdictional powers.

2. **Judicial Authority**: Regional and District Councils have appellate powers over village councils, with limited jurisdiction for other courts, emphasizing the autonomy of local governance in tribal areas.

3. **Administrative Powers**: Councils can create rules for the functioning of village councils and courts, including procedures for trials and appeals, and the enforcement of decisions.

4. **Financial Management**: Establishment of District and Regional Funds for managing finances, including the power to assess land revenue and impose taxes, is granted to the councils.

5. **Regulatory Powers**: Councils can regulate money-lending and trading by non-tribals, ensuring that local economic activities align with tribal interests.

6. **Application of State and Central Laws**: Provisions are made for the application of state and central laws in autonomous regions, allowing councils to direct the applicability of certain laws.

7. **Oversight and Accountability**: The Governor has the authority to annul or suspend acts of councils if they threaten public order, and can appoint commissions to report on the administration of these regions.

8. **Dissolution of Councils**: The Governor can dissolve councils based on recommendations from appointed commissions, with provisions for re-elections or direct administration.

Overall, the document emphasizes the autonomy of tribal governance while ensuring oversight and integration with state and national legal frameworks.

nodes.title: Dissolution of a District or a Regional Council.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines provisions related to the governance of autonomous districts and regional councils in India, specifically under the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution. Key points include:

1. **Dissolution of Councils**: The Governor has the authority to dissolve a District or Regional Council based on a Commission's recommendation, with options for immediate elections or temporary administration by the Governor or a designated body.

2. **Assumption of Powers**: The Governor can assume the functions of a District or Regional Council if he determines that the administration cannot be conducted as per the Schedule, with provisions for extending this assumption.

3. **Exclusion from Constituencies**: The Governor can declare certain areas within autonomous districts as not part of specific constituencies for legislative assembly elections, allowing for flexibility in electoral arrangements.

4. **Transitional Provisions**: Until District Councils are constituted, the Governor will administer autonomous districts, with the power to regulate laws and make regulations for governance in these areas.

5. **Amendments and Provisions**: The document references amendments and specific provisions applicable to states like Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram, including the establishment of an Interim Executive Council for the Bodoland Territorial Areas District.

Overall, the document emphasizes the Governor's significant role in the administration and governance of autonomous regions, ensuring that local councils can be reconstituted or managed effectively in response to changing circumstances.

nodes.summary: The partial document outlines specific provisions from the Constitution of India, particularly focusing on miscellaneous articles. It discusses the abolition of the privy purse as per the Twenty-sixth Amendment Act of 1971, extinguishing all rights related to it for former rulers. It also details the President's authority to modify the application of laws concerning major ports and aerodromes, including the definitions of these terms. Additionally, it addresses the consequences of a state's failure to comply with directions from the Union, allowing the President to determine if the state government can function according to constitutional provisions. Lastly, it provides a definition of "agricultural income" as it pertains to Indian income tax laws.

(Part XIX.—MISCELLANEOUS)
222
(b) on and from the commencement of the Constitution (Twenty-
sixth Amendment) Act, 1971, privy purse is abolished and all rights, 
liabilities and obligations in respect of privy purse are extinguished and 
accordingly the Ruler or, as the case may be, the successor of such 
Ruler, referred to in clause (a) or any other person shall not be paid any 
sum as privy purse.]
364. Special provisions as to major ports and aerodromes.—(1) 
Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, the President may by public 
notification direct that as from such date as may be specified in the 
notification— 
(a) any law made by Parliament or by the Legislature of a State 
shall not apply to any major port or aerodrome or shall apply thereto 
subject to such exceptions or modifications as may be specified in the 
notification; or 
(b) any existing law shall cease to have effect in any major port or 
aerodrome except as respects things done or omitted to be done before 
the said date, or shall in its application to such port or aerodrome have 
effect subject to such exceptions or modifications as may be specified in 
the notification.
(2) In this article—
(a) “major port” means a port declared to be a major port by or 
under any law made by Parliament or any existing law and includes all 
areas for the time being included within the limits of such port;
(b) “aerodrome” means aerodrome as defined for the purposes of 
the enactments relating to airways, aircraft and air navigation.
365. Effect of failure to comply with, or to give effect to, directions 
given by the Union.—Where any State has failed to comply with, or to give 
effect to, any directions given in the exercise of the executive power of the Union 
under any of the provisions of this Constitution, it shall be lawful for the 
President to hold that a situation has arisen in which the Government of the State 
cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of this Constitution.
366. Definitions.—In this Constitution, unless the context otherwise 
requires, the following expressions have the meanings hereby respectively 
assigned to them, that is to say—

374. Provisions as to Judges of the Federal Court and proceedings 
pending in the Federal Court or before His Majesty in Council.—(1) The 
Judges of the Federal Court holding office immediately before the 
commencement of this Constitution shall, unless they have elected otherwise, 
become on such commencement the Judges of the Supreme Court and shall 
thereupon be entitled to such salaries and allowances and to such rights in 
respect of leave of absence and pension as are provided for under article 125 in 
respect of the Judges of the Supreme Court.
(2) All suits, appeals and proceedings, civil or criminal, pending in the 
Federal Court at the commencement of this Constitution shall stand removed to 
the Supreme Court, and the Supreme Court shall have jurisdiction to hear and 
determine the same, and the judgments and  orders of the Federal Court delivered 
or made before the  commencement of this Constitution shall have the same force 
and effect as if they had been delivered or made by the Supreme Court.
(3) Nothing in this Constitution shall operate to invalidate the exercise of 
jurisdiction by His Majesty in Council to dispose of appeals and petitions from, 
or in respect of, any judgment, decree or order of any court within the territory 
of India in so far as the exercise of such jurisdiction is authorised by law, and 
any order of His Majesty in Council made on any such appeal or petition after 
the commencement of this Constitution shall for all purposes have effect as if it 
were an order or decree made by the Supreme Court in the exercise of the  
jurisdiction conferred on such Court by this Constitution.
(4) On and from the commencement of this Constitution the jurisdiction of 
the authority functioning as the Privy Council in a State specified in Part B of the 
First Schedule to entertain and dispose of appeals and petitions from or in respect 
of any judgment, decree or order of any court within that State shall cease, and all 
appeals and other proceedings pending before the said authority at such 
commencement shall be transferred to, and disposed of by, the Supreme Court.
(5) Further provision may be made by Parliament by law to give effect to 
the provisions of this article.

PART XXII
SHORT TITLE, COMMENCEMENT, 1[AUTHORITATIVE 
TEXT IN HINDI] AND REPEALS
393. Short title.—This Constitution may be called the Constitution of 
India. 
394.  Commencement.—This article and articles 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60,  324, 
366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392 and 393 shall come into force at once, and 
the remaining provisions of this Constitution shall come into force on the 
twenty-sixth day of January, 1950, which day is referred to in this Constitution 
as the commencement of this Constitution. 
2[394A. Authoritative text in the Hindi language.—(1) The President 
shall cause to be published under his authority,— 
(a) the translation of this Constitution in the Hindi language, 
signed by the members of the Constituent Assembly, with such 
modifications as may be necessary to bring it in conformity with the 
language, style and terminology adopted in the authoritative texts of 
Central Acts in the Hindi language, and incorporating therein all the 
amendments of this Constitution made before such publication; and
(b) the translation in the Hindi language of every amendment of 
this Constitution made in the English language. 
(2) The translation of this Constitution and of every amendment thereof 
published under clause (1) shall be construed to have the same meaning as  the 
original thereof and if any difficulty arises in so construing any part of such 
translation, the President shall cause the same to be revised suitably.
(3) The translation of this Constitution and of every amendment thereof 
published under this article shall  be deemed to be, for all purposes, the 
authoritative text thereof in the Hindi language.]
395. Repeals.—
The Indian Independence Act, 1947, and the 
Government of India Act, 1935, together with all enactments amending or 
supplementing the latter Act, but not including the Abolition of Privy Council 
Jurisdiction Act, 1949, are hereby repealed.

PART XX AMENDMENT OF THE CONSTITUTION
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines the procedures and powers of Parliament to amend the Constitution of India as specified in Article 368. It details the process for initiating amendments, which requires the introduction of a Bill in either House of Parliament, passing by a majority of total membership and a two-thirds majority of those present and voting. Certain amendments, particularly those affecting specific articles and provisions, require ratification by at least half of the State Legislatures. The document also states that amendments cannot be challenged in court and emphasizes that there are no limitations on Parliament's power to amend the Constitution. Additionally, it introduces temporary provisions allowing Parliament to legislate on certain matters in the State List as if they were in the Concurrent List for a period of five years.

PART XX
AMENDMENT OF THE CONSTITUTION
368. 
1[Power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and 
procedure therefor].— 2[(1) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, 
Parliament may in exercise of its constituent power amend by way of addition, 
variation or repeal any provision of this Constitution in accordance with the 
procedure laid down in this article.] 
3[(2)] An amendment of this Constitution may be initiated only by the 
introduction of a Bill for the purpose in either House of Parliament, and when 
the Bill is passed in each House by a majority of the total membership of that 
House and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that 
House present and voting, 4[it shall be presented to the President who shall give 
his assent to the Bill and thereupon] the Constitution shall stand amended in 
accordance with the terms of the Bill:
Provided that if such amendment seeks to make any change in—
(a) article 54, article 55, article 73, 5[ article 162, article 241 or 
article 279A]; or
  (b) Chapter IV of Part V, Chapter V of Part VI, or Chapter I of Part XI; or
(c) any of the Lists in the Seventh Schedule; or
(d) the representation of States in Parliament; or
(e) the provisions of this article,

PART XXI
1[TEMPORARY, TRANSITIONAL AND 
SPECIAL PROVISIONS] 
369. Temporary power to Parliament to make laws with respect to 
certain matters in the State List as if they were matters in the Concurrent 
List.—Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament shall, during 
a period of five years from the commencement of this Constitution, have power 
to make laws with respect to the following matters as if they were enumerated 
in the Concurrent List, namely:— 
(a) trade and commerce within a State in, and the production, supply 
and distribution of, cotton and woollen textiles, raw cotton (including 
ginned cotton and unginned cotton or kapas), cotton seed, paper 
(including newsprint), food-stuffs (including edible oilseeds and oil), 
cattle fodder (including oil-cakes and other concentrates), coal 
(including coke and derivatives of coal), iron, steel and mica;
(b) offences against laws with respect to any of the matters mentioned
in clause (a), jurisdiction and powers of all courts except the Supreme 
Court with respect to any of those matters, and fees in respect of any of 
those matters but not including fees taken in any court,
but any law made by Parliament, which Parliament would not but for the 
provisions of this article have been competent to make, shall, to the extent of the 
incompetency, cease to have effect on the expiration of the said period, except as

370. Temporary provisions with respect to the State of Jammu and Kashmir.
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses specific provisions of the Constitution of India related to the State of Jammu and Kashmir and other states, focusing on temporary, transitional, and special provisions. It outlines the limitations on Parliament's power to legislate for Jammu and Kashmir, emphasizing the need for consultation with the state government and the President's authority to declare certain articles operative or inoperative. The document also mentions modifications to Article 370, which previously granted special status to Jammu and Kashmir, and details the special provisions for states like Maharashtra, Gujarat, and Nagaland, including the establishment of development boards and the autonomy of local customs and laws. Overall, it highlights the unique constitutional status and governance arrangements for these regions within India.

It details the responsibilities of the President and the Governor in these states, including the establishment of development boards, equitable allocation of funds, and provisions for technical education and employment opportunities in Maharashtra and Gujarat. nodes.title: 371A. Special provision with respect to the State of Nagaland.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines specific provisions related to the governance and administration of the State of Nagaland, particularly focusing on the role and responsibilities of the Governor. Key points include:

1. The Governor's special responsibility for law and order in Nagaland, particularly in the Naga Hills-Tuensang Area, and the exercise of individual judgment in this regard.
2. The establishment of a regional council for the Tuensang district, detailing its composition, member selection, qualifications, term of office, and operational procedures.
3. The Governor's authority to administer the Tuensang district for a specified period, including the allocation of funds from the Government of India and the application of legislative acts.
4. The appointment of a Minister for Tuensang affairs, who will have direct access to the Governor and responsibility for matters related to the district.
5. Provisions for the adaptation of legislative assembly representation and electoral processes specific to Nagaland.
6. The President's power to address any difficulties in implementing these provisions within a defined timeframe. 

Overall, the document emphasizes the unique administrative framework established for Nagaland, reflecting its special status within the Indian Constitution.

nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines special provisions in the Constitution of India concerning various states, particularly focusing on Maharashtra, Gujarat, Nagaland, Assam, Manipur, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, and Sikkim. Key points include:

1. **Maharashtra and Gujarat**: The President can assign special responsibilities to the Governors for establishing development boards, equitable fund allocation, and providing technical education and employment opportunities in specific regions.

2. **Nagaland**: The document specifies that certain parliamentary acts do not apply unless the Nagaland Legislative Assembly decides otherwise. The Governor has special responsibilities regarding law and order and the administration of the Tuensang district, including the establishment of a regional council.

3. **Assam and Manipur**: Provisions for the constitution and functions of committees within the Legislative Assemblies to represent tribal and hill areas, ensuring proper governance and administration.

4. **Andhra Pradesh and Telangana**: The President can create orders for equitable opportunities in public employment and education, and establish an Administrative Tribunal to oversee civil service matters, including appointments and promotions.

5. **Sikkim**: The document details the formation of the Legislative Assembly, representation in the House of the People, and the Governor's responsibilities for ensuring social and economic advancement for different population sections.

Overall, the document emphasizes the unique administrative and governance structures tailored to the specific needs and contexts of these states.

nodes.title: 371F. Special provisions with respect to the State of Sikkim.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines specific provisions related to the State of Sikkim and other northeastern states of India, as part of the Constitution of India. Key points include:

1. **Legislative Assembly**: The duration of the Legislative Assembly for Sikkim is set to four years, starting from the appointed day, with provisions for one parliamentary constituency.
2. **Representation**: The representative for Sikkim in the House of the People will be elected by the members of the Sikkim Legislative Assembly.
3. **Protection of Rights**: Provisions are made for ensuring representation of different population sections in the Legislative Assembly and for delimiting constituencies accordingly.
4. **Governor's Responsibilities**: The Governor of Sikkim is tasked with ensuring peace and equitable social and economic advancement for various population sections.
5. **Continuity of Government Functions**: Existing courts, authorities, and laws in Sikkim will continue to function until amended or repealed, with adaptations possible by the President for alignment with the Constitution.
6. **Jurisdiction Limitations**: The Supreme Court and other courts will not have jurisdiction over disputes related to treaties or agreements concerning Sikkim made before the appointed day.
7. **Special Provisions for Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh**: The document also includes special provisions for Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh, emphasizing local customs, laws, and the Governor's responsibilities regarding law and order.

Overall, the document establishes a framework for the governance and legal structure of Sikkim and other northeastern states, ensuring local customs and representation are respected within the broader constitutional framework.

nodes.title: 371G. Special provision with respect to the State of Mizoram.
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines specific provisions in the Constitution of India related to temporary, transitional, and special arrangements for certain states. It includes details about the validity of actions taken in Sikkim prior to the Constitution (Thirty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1975. It also specifies special provisions for the states of Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, and Karnataka. For Mizoram, it states that certain parliamentary acts do not apply unless the state assembly decides otherwise, and it mandates a minimum number of assembly members. Arunachal Pradesh's provisions grant the Governor special responsibilities regarding law and order, with the Governor's discretion being final in related matters. Goa's provision establishes a minimum assembly size, while Karnataka's provisions allow the President to assign special responsibilities to the Governor for regional development, including equitable resource allocation and educational opportunities for the Hyderabad-Karnataka region.
