nodes.title: 373. Power of the President to adapt laws.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines specific provisions of the Constitution of India related to temporary, transitional, and special arrangements for certain states. It includes:

1. **Validity of Actions in Sikkim**: Actions taken in Sikkim before the Constitution (Thirty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1975, are deemed valid if they conform to the amended Constitution.

2. **Special Provisions for Mizoram**: Parliament's laws regarding religious practices, customary law, and land ownership in Mizoram require the state assembly's resolution to apply.

3. **Special Provisions for Arunachal Pradesh**: The Governor has special responsibilities regarding law and order, with the authority to act based on individual judgment after consulting the Council of Ministers.

4. **Legislative Assembly Composition**: The document specifies the minimum number of members for the Legislative Assemblies of Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh, and Goa.

5. **Special Provisions for Karnataka**: The President can assign special responsibilities to the Governor for the Hyderabad-Karnataka region, including the establishment of a development board and equitable allocation of resources.

6. **Continuance of Existing Laws**: Existing laws remain in force until altered or repealed, with provisions for the President to adapt laws to align with the new Constitution.

7. **Judicial Provisions**: Judges of the Federal Court transition to the Supreme Court, and ongoing legal proceedings are transferred to the Supreme Court, maintaining the validity of prior judgments.

Overall, the document emphasizes the unique legal and administrative frameworks established for specific states within India, ensuring their customs and governance are respected while integrating them into the broader constitutional framework.

pending in the Federal Court or before His Majesty in Council.—(1) The 
Judges of the Federal Court holding office immediately before the 
commencement of this Constitution shall, unless they have elected otherwise,

nodes.title: 374. Provisions as to Judges of the Federal Court and proceedings pending in the Federal Court or before His Majesty in Council.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines specific temporary, transitional, and special provisions of the Constitution of India, particularly focusing on the powers and roles of various judicial and governmental authorities following the Constitution's commencement. Key points include:

1. **Preventive Detention**: The President has the authority to make orders regarding preventive detention until Parliament enacts relevant provisions.
2. **Judges of the Federal Court**: Judges in office before the Constitution's commencement automatically become Judges of the Supreme Court, with their existing rights and salaries preserved.
3. **Pending Proceedings**: All legal proceedings pending in the Federal Court are transferred to the Supreme Court, which will have jurisdiction over them.
4. **Privy Council Jurisdiction**: The jurisdiction of the Privy Council in certain states ceases, with pending appeals transferred to the Supreme Court.
5. **Continuity of Courts and Authorities**: All existing courts and authorities will continue to function under the new Constitution.
6. **Judges of High Courts**: Judges of High Courts before the Constitution's commencement will transition to corresponding High Courts, retaining their rights and salaries.
7. **Comptroller and Auditor-General**: The existing Auditor-General will become the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India, maintaining their rights and term of office.

These provisions ensure a smooth transition to the new constitutional framework while preserving the roles and responsibilities of existing judicial and governmental entities.

2. **Judges of High Courts**: Provisions regarding the transition of High Court judges from their previous roles to their new positions under the Constitution, including eligibility for Chief Justice roles and entitlements related to salaries and pensions.
3. **Comptroller and Auditor-General**: The existing Auditor-General will transition to the role of Comptroller and Auditor-General with specified rights and entitlements.

6. **Omissions**: Several provisions related to provisional Parliament, the President, and Governors of Provinces have been omitted by subsequent amendments.

anything in clause (2) of article 217, the Judges of a High Court in any

The partial document outlines specific temporary, transitional, and special provisions of the Constitution of India, particularly focusing on the continuity of various judicial and administrative roles following the Constitution's commencement. Key points include:

1. **Continuation of Courts and Authorities**: All courts and authorities in India will continue to function under the new Constitution.
2. **Judges of High Courts**: Provisions for judges of High Courts transitioning to their roles in corresponding states, including eligibility for Chief Justice positions and entitlements regarding salaries and pensions.
3. **Comptroller and Auditor-General**: The existing Auditor-General will transition to the role of Comptroller and Auditor-General with specified rights and entitlements.
4. **Public Service Commissions**: Members of existing Public Service Commissions will continue in their roles under the new Constitution unless they choose otherwise.
5. **Special Provision for Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly**: A specific provision regarding the duration of the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly, allowing it to function for five years unless dissolved sooner.
6. **Omissions**: Several provisions related to provisional Parliament, the President, and Governors of Provinces have been omitted by amendments.

Overall, the document emphasizes the preservation of existing governmental structures and roles during the transition to the new constitutional framework.

PART XXII
SHORT TITLE, COMMENCEMENT, 1[AUTHORITATIVE 
TEXT IN HINDI] AND REPEALS
393. Short title.—This Constitution may be called the Constitution of 
India. 
394.  Commencement.—This article and articles 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60,  324, 
366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392 and 393 shall come into force at once, and 
the remaining provisions of this Constitution shall come into force on the 
twenty-sixth day of January, 1950, which day is referred to in this Constitution 
as the commencement of this Constitution. 
2[394A. Authoritative text in the Hindi language.—(1) The President 
shall cause to be published under his authority,— 
(a) the translation of this Constitution in the Hindi language, 
signed by the members of the Constituent Assembly, with such 
modifications as may be necessary to bring it in conformity with the 
language, style and terminology adopted in the authoritative texts of 
Central Acts in the Hindi language, and incorporating therein all the 
amendments of this Constitution made before such publication; and
(b) the translation in the Hindi language of every amendment of 
this Constitution made in the English language. 
(2) The translation of this Constitution and of every amendment thereof 
published under clause (1) shall be construed to have the same meaning as  the 
original thereof and if any difficulty arises in so construing any part of such 
translation, the President shall cause the same to be revised suitably.
(3) The translation of this Constitution and of every amendment thereof 
published under this article shall  be deemed to be, for all purposes, the 
authoritative text thereof in the Hindi language.]
395. Repeals.—
The Indian Independence Act, 1947, and the 
Government of India Act, 1935, together with all enactments amending or 
supplementing the latter Act, but not including the Abolition of Privy Council 
Jurisdiction Act, 1949, are hereby repealed.

nodes.summary: The partial document outlines the First Schedule of the Constitution of India, detailing the names and territories of various states. It specifies the territories included in each state, referencing various acts and amendments that have influenced territorial boundaries over time. Key states mentioned include Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Gujarat, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Odisha, Punjab, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal, Nagaland, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Manipur, Tripura, Meghalaya, Sikkim, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh, and Goa. The document highlights the historical context of territorial changes and the legal framework governing these adjustments, including exclusions and specific provisions from various legislative acts.

nodes.title: SECOND SCHEDULE [Articles 59(3), 65(3), 75(6), 97, 125, 148(3), 158(3), 164 (5), 186 and 221]
PART A PROVISIONS AS TO THE PRESIDENT AND THE GOVERNORS OF STATES
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines provisions related to the emoluments, allowances, and privileges of the President of India and the Governors of States, as well as the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the House of the People and the Council of States. It specifies the monthly salaries for the President (10,000 rupees) and Governors (5,500 rupees), along with allowances that were previously applicable to the Governor-General and provincial governors before the Constitution's commencement. It also states that individuals acting in these roles are entitled to the same benefits as the officials they replace. Additionally, it details the salaries and allowances for the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the House of the People and the Council of States, as well as for the legislative assembly and council of states, referencing the compensation that was in place prior to the Constitution.

nodes.summary: The partial document outlines provisions related to the salaries and allowances of key legislative and judicial figures in India as specified in the Constitution. It details the compensation for the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the House of the People, the Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Council of States, as well as the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Legislative Assembly and the Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Legislative Council of a State. The document specifies that their salaries will be equivalent to those previously paid to their counterparts in the Constituent Assembly and corresponding provincial assemblies before the Constitution's commencement. Additionally, it includes provisions for the salaries of Supreme Court judges, detailing specific amounts for the Chief Justice and other judges, along with conditions regarding pension adjustments and the provision of official residences for judges.

nodes.title: PART D PROVISIONS AS TO THE JUDGES OF THE SUPREME COURT AND OF THE HIGH COURTS
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines provisions related to the salaries, allowances, and conditions of service for the Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts in India, as specified in the Second Schedule of the Constitution. It details the monthly salary rates for the Chief Justice and other judges, stipulating reductions in salary for those receiving pensions from previous government service. It also mentions the entitlement of judges to official residences without rent, travel allowances, and the governance of their leave and pension rights based on prior provisions applicable to the Federal Court judges. Additionally, it includes similar provisions for the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India, highlighting their salary and conditions of service. The document reflects amendments made over time, indicating changes in salary figures and conditions.

nodes.title: FIFTH SCHEDULE [Article 244(1)]
Provisions as to the Administration and Control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines the provisions related to the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in India, as specified in the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution. It includes several key points:

1. **General Provisions**: Defines the term "State" in the context of Scheduled Areas, clarifying that it excludes certain northeastern states. It establishes that the executive power of a State extends to Scheduled Areas and mandates the Governor to report to the President on their administration.

2. **Tribes Advisory Council**: Establishes the requirement for a Tribes Advisory Council in states with Scheduled Areas, detailing its composition, duties, and the Governor's authority to regulate its functioning.

3. **Law Applicability**: Grants the Governor the power to exempt certain laws from applying to Scheduled Areas or to modify their application, as well as to create regulations for governance in these areas, particularly concerning land transfer and business practices.

4. **Scheduled Areas Definition**: Defines "Scheduled Areas" and outlines the President's authority to declare, modify, or rescind such areas, including provisions for boundary adjustments and the creation of new Scheduled Areas.

5. **Amendment of the Schedule**: Allows Parliament to amend the provisions of the Fifth Schedule without it being considered a constitutional amendment under Article 368.

Overall, the document emphasizes the governance framework for Scheduled Areas and the rights and protections for Scheduled Tribes, ensuring their welfare and advancement through structured administrative mechanisms.

It details the authority of Regional and District Councils to establish village councils or courts for resolving disputes among Scheduled Tribes, excluding certain cases. It specifies that these councils have exclusive jurisdiction over such matters, with appeals directed to the Regional or District Councils, and only the High Court and Supreme Court retaining jurisdiction over specific cases as designated by the Governor. nodes.title: Administration of justice in autonomous districts and autonomous regions.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines provisions related to the administration of justice in autonomous districts and regions as specified in the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution of India. Key points include:

1. **Law Submission and Effect**: Laws made under the specified provisions must be submitted to the Governor for assent before taking effect.

2. **Village Councils and Courts**: Regional and District Councils can establish village councils or courts to handle disputes among Scheduled Tribes, excluding certain cases. They have the authority to appoint members and presiding officers for these councils and courts.

3. **Court Jurisdiction**: The Regional or District Councils have appellate jurisdiction over cases tried by village councils, with the High Court and Supreme Court retaining jurisdiction over specified matters.

4. **Rule-Making Authority**: Councils can create rules regarding the constitution and powers of village councils and courts, trial procedures, and enforcement of decisions, subject to the Governor's approval.

5. **Governor's Powers**: The Governor can confer powers under the Code of Civil Procedure and the Code of Criminal Procedure to District and Regional Councils for specific cases and may withdraw or modify these powers.

6. **Establishment of Local Institutions**: District Councils can establish and manage primary schools, dispensaries, and other local institutions, with regulations subject to the Governor's approval.

7. **Financial Provisions**: Each autonomous district and region will have designated funds to manage financial resources received by the respective councils for administration.

Overall, the document emphasizes the autonomy of local councils in governance and justice administration while outlining the oversight role of the Governor.

nodes.title: District and Regional Funds.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines provisions related to the governance and administrative powers of autonomous districts and regions in India as specified in the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution. Key points include:

1. **Governor's Authority**: The Governor has the power to confer certain functions to District and Regional Councils, including the establishment and management of primary schools, dispensaries, and infrastructure.

2. **District and Regional Funds**: Each autonomous district and region is to have its own fund, which will manage financial resources received from various administrative activities. The Governor can set rules for the management of these funds.

3. **Taxation Powers**: District and Regional Councils are empowered to assess and collect land revenue and impose taxes on various activities, including professions, trades, and the entry of goods into markets.

4. **Regulation of Money-Lending and Trading**: District Councils can regulate money-lending and trading by non-tribals, including licensing requirements and interest rate limits.

5. **Application of State and Parliamentary Laws**: The document specifies conditions under which laws made by the State Legislature or Parliament apply to autonomous districts and regions, allowing for exceptions and modifications as directed by the District Councils or the Governor.

6. **Publication of Regulations**: All laws and regulations made by the District or Regional Councils must be published in the Official Gazette to have legal effect.

These provisions aim to empower local governance in specific regions while maintaining oversight by the state and central authorities.

It details the types of taxes that can be levied, including those on goods entering markets, maintenance of public services, and entertainment. The document also discusses the sharing of mineral royalties between the state government and District Councils, including dispute resolution by the Governor. Additionally, it addresses the District Council's authority to regulate money-lending and trading activities by non-tribals, specifying licensing requirements, interest rate limits, and account maintenance for money-lenders. Amendments to these provisions are noted, reflecting changes in application to specific states.

nodes.title: Power of District Council to make regulations for the control of money-lending and trading by non-tribals.
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines provisions related to the regulation of money-lending and trading by non-tribals in autonomous districts of India, as specified in the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution. It grants the District Council the authority to create regulations governing these activities, including licensing requirements for money-lenders and traders, setting maximum interest rates, and maintaining account records. The document also mentions amendments to these provisions for specific states, such as Tripura, Mizoram, and Assam, and emphasizes that regulations must be approved by a majority of the District Council and the Governor before taking effect. Additionally, it mandates the publication of laws and regulations in the Official Gazette to ensure they have the force of law.

110. Power of District Council to make regulations for the control 
of money-lending  and  trading  by non-tribals.—(1)  The  District  
Council   of  an   autonomous  district  may   make regulations  for  the 
regulation and control of money-lending or trading within the district by 
persons other than Scheduled Tribes resident in the district.
(2) In particular and without prejudice to the generality of the 
foregoing power, such regulations may— 
(a) prescribe that no one except the holder of a licence issued 
in that behalf shall   carry on the business of money-lending;
(b) prescribe the maximum rate of interest which may be 
charged or be recovered by a money-lender;
(c) provide for the maintenance of accounts by money-lenders 
and for the inspection of such accounts by officers appointed in that 
behalf by the District Council;
(d) prescribe that no person who is not a member of the 
Scheduled Tribes resident in the district shall carry on wholesale or 
retail business in any commodity except under a licence issued in that 
behalf by the District Council:

nodes.title: Publication of laws, rules and regulations made under the Schedule.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines provisions related to the governance and administration of autonomous districts and regions in India, specifically under the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution. Key points include:

1. **Regulation Making**: District Councils can make regulations, which require a three-fourths majority for approval and must be submitted to the Governor for assent before taking effect.

2. **Publication of Laws**: All laws and regulations made by District or Regional Councils must be published in the Official Gazette to have legal force.

3. **Application of State and Parliamentary Acts**: Specific provisions detail how Acts of the State Legislature and Parliament apply to autonomous districts, allowing District Councils to direct the applicability of certain laws and providing the Governor with the authority to exempt or modify their application.

4. **Financial Management**: Estimated receipts and expenditures for autonomous districts must be discussed by the District Council and presented separately in the State's annual financial statement.

5. **Commission for Administration Review**: The Governor can appoint a Commission to report on the administration of autonomous districts, focusing on education, medical facilities, and legislative needs.

6. **Governor's Powers**: The Governor has the authority to annul or suspend acts and resolutions of District Councils if they threaten public safety or order, and can dissolve councils based on recommendations from a Commission.

7. **Elections and Constituencies**: The Governor can declare certain areas within autonomous districts as not part of specific constituencies for legislative assembly elections.

Overall, the document emphasizes the autonomy of local councils while also outlining the oversight and regulatory powers of the Governor and the State Legislature.

nodes.title: Application of Acts of Parliament and of the Legislature of the State of Meghalaya to autonomous districts and autonomous regions in the State of Meghalaya.
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the provisions of the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution of India, specifically focusing on the application of laws in autonomous districts and regions within the states of Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram. It outlines the authority of District and Regional Councils to make laws on specified matters, and establishes that if any law made by these councils conflicts with state legislation, the state law will prevail. Additionally, it details the powers of the President and Governors to exempt certain Acts of Parliament or state legislation from applying to these autonomous areas, allowing for modifications or exceptions as deemed necessary. The document emphasizes the autonomy of these regions in legislative matters, particularly concerning the consumption of non-distilled alcoholic liquor.

5. The Governor's ability to annul or suspend acts and resolutions of District and Regional Councils if they threaten national safety or public order, including the procedure for legislative oversight of such actions.

nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses provisions related to the administration of autonomous districts in India as outlined in the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution. Key points include:

1. The Governor's authority to assume functions of the District or Regional Council if the administration cannot be conducted as per the Schedule, with the possibility of extending this authority for up to six months.
2. The requirement for any order made by the Governor to be presented to the State Legislature, which must approve it within thirty days for it to remain in effect.
3. The Governor's power to exclude certain areas from autonomous districts for the purpose of forming constituencies for elections to the Legislative Assemblies of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram.
4. Transitional provisions for the establishment of District Councils, where the Governor temporarily administers the district until a council is formed, including the ability to regulate laws applicable to the area.
5. Specific amendments and provisions related to the Bodoland Territorial Areas District, including the formation of an Interim Executive Council and representation for non-tribal communities.

nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines the provisions related to the administration of tribal areas in the states of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram as per the Sixth Schedule of the Indian Constitution. Key points include:

1. **Autonomous Districts and Regions**: It establishes that tribal areas are designated as autonomous districts, with the Governor having the authority to create autonomous regions within these districts based on the presence of different Scheduled Tribes.

2. **Governor's Powers**: The Governor can modify the boundaries of autonomous districts, create new districts, and make other administrative changes, subject to certain conditions and the consideration of reports from appointed commissions.

3. **District and Regional Councils**: Each autonomous district will have a District Council, consisting of elected and nominated members, while autonomous regions will have Regional Councils. These councils are responsible for local governance and administration.

4. **Legislative Powers**: The councils have the authority to make laws on various matters, including land use, agriculture, education, and public health, with certain laws requiring the Governor's assent before taking effect.

5. **Administration of Justice**: The councils can establish village councils or courts to handle disputes among Scheduled Tribes, with limited jurisdiction over such cases, and the High Court retains oversight in specified matters.

6. **Elections and Governance**: The document details the electoral process for council members, their term lengths, and the procedures for conducting business within the councils, emphasizing the need for rules to be established in consultation with tribal organizations.

Overall, the document emphasizes the autonomy and self-governance of tribal areas while outlining the framework for their administration and legislative powers.

nodes.summary: The partial document discusses Article 370 of the Constitution of India, which pertains to the special status of the State of Jammu and Kashmir. It outlines the temporary provisions that were in place regarding the state's governance and the limitations on Parliament's power to legislate for Jammu and Kashmir. The document highlights the President's authority to declare modifications to Article 370, particularly noting that as of August 6, 2019, most clauses of Article 370 ceased to be operative, allowing all provisions of the Constitution to apply to Jammu and Kashmir without exceptions. Additionally, it references a previous modification made in 1952 regarding the definition of the state government.

(Part XXI.—Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions)

1[370. Temporary provisions with respect  to the State of Jammu 
and Kashmir.—(1) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution,— 
(a) the provisions of article 238 shall not apply in relation to the State 
of  Jammu and Kashmir; 
(b) the power of Parliament to make laws for the said State shall be 
limited to—
(i) those matters in the Union List and  the Concurrent List 
which, in consultation with the Government of the State, are declared 
by the President to correspond to matters specified in the Instrument 
of Accession governing the accession of the State to the Dominion  of 
India as the matters with respect to which the Dominion Legislature 
may make laws for that State; and
______________________________________________
In exercise of the powers conferred by clause (3) of article 370 read with clause (1) of 
article 370 of the Constitution of India, the President, on the recommendation of 
Parliament, is pleased to declare that, as from the 6th August, 2019 all clauses of said 
article 370 shall cease to be operative except the following which shall read as under, 
namely:—
“370. All provisions of this Constitution, as amended from time to time, 
without any modifications or exceptions, shall apply to the State of Jammu and 
Kashmir notwithstanding anything contrary contained in article 152 or article 308 or 
any other article of this Constitution or any other provision of the Constitution of 
Jammu and Kashmir or any law, document, judgment, ordinance, order, by-law, rule, 
regulation, notification, custom or usage having the force of law in the territory of 
India, or any other instrument, treaty or agreement as envisaged under article 363 or 
otherwise.”.
(See Appendix III) (C.O. 273).
1. In exercise of the powers conferred by clause (3) of the Constitution of India, the

and Kashmir, declared that, as from the 17th day of November, 1952, the said art. 370 
shall be operative with the modification that for the Explanation in cl. (1) thereof, the 
following Explanation is substituted, namely:—
“Explanation.–For the purposes of this article, the Government of the State means 
the person for the time being recognised by the President on the recommendation of 
the Legislative Assembly of the State as the *Sadar-I-Riyasat of Jammu and Kashmir, 
acting on the advice of the Council of Ministers of the State for the time being in 
office.”.
(C.O. 44, dated the 15th November, 1952).

nodes.summary: The partial document discusses provisions related to the administration of autonomous districts and regions in the State of Mizoram as outlined in the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution of India. Key points include the President's authority to exempt certain Acts of Parliament from applying to these autonomous areas, the requirement for estimated receipts and expenditures of these districts to be presented separately in the state's annual financial statement, and the Governor's power to appoint a Commission to investigate and report on various administrative matters concerning these districts. The Commission's focus includes evaluating educational and medical facilities, the need for new legislation, and the administration of laws by local councils. Additionally, there are references to amendments and changes in the application of these provisions over time.

or an autonomous region in the State of Mizoram, or shall apply to

or modifications as he may specify in the notification and any such 
direction may be given so as to have retrospective effect.]] 
13. Estimated receipts and expenditure pertaining to autonomous 
districts to be shown separately in the annual financial statement.—The 
estimated receipts and expenditure pertaining to an autonomous district 
which are to be credited to, or is to be made from, the Consolidated Fund of 
the State 1*** shall be first placed before the District Council for discussion 
and then after such discussion be shown separately in the annual financial 
statement of the State to be laid before the Legislature of the State under 
article 202. 
214. Appointment of Commission to inquire into and report on 
the administration of autonomous districts and autonomous regions.—
(1) The Governor may at any time appoint a Commission to examine and 
report on any matter specified by him relating to the administration of the 
autonomous districts and autonomous regions in the State, including matters 
specified in clauses (c), (d), (e) and (f) of sub-paragraph (3) of paragraph 1 
of this Schedule, or may appoint a Commission to inquire into and report 
from time to time on the administration of autonomous districts and 
autonomous regions in the State generally and in particular on—
(a) the provision of educational and medical facilities and 
communications in such districts and regions;
(b) the need for any new or special legislation in respect of 
such districts and regions; and
(c) the administration of the laws, rules and regulations made 
by the District and Regional Councils;
and define the procedure to be followed by such Commission.

nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines the State List from the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution of India, detailing the subjects on which state governments have the authority to legislate. Key points include:

1. **Public Order and Police**: States have jurisdiction over public order (excluding military intervention) and police forces.
2. **Judicial Matters**: It covers the administration of courts, including High Courts and local courts, and related fees.
3. **Prisons and Rehabilitation**: States manage prisons and reformatories, including arrangements with other states for their use.
4. **Local Government**: It addresses the structure and powers of local self-governments and municipal authorities.
5. **Public Health**: States are responsible for public health, sanitation, and healthcare facilities.
6. **Cultural and Religious Affairs**: It includes provisions for local pilgrimages and the management of libraries and historical monuments.
7. **Agriculture and Animal Husbandry**: The list covers agricultural practices, veterinary services, and land management.
8. **Water and Irrigation**: States oversee water supply, irrigation, and related infrastructure.
9. **Trade and Commerce**: It includes regulations on trade within the state and industries, subject to certain central provisions.

Overall, the document delineates the powers and responsibilities of state governments in various sectors, emphasizing local governance and administration.

nodes.text:
THE CONSTITUTION OF  INDIA
(Part XIX.—MISCELLANEOUS)
220
1[361A. Protection of publication of proceedings of Parliament and 
State Legislatures.—(1) No person shall be liable to any proceedings, civil or 
criminal, in any court in respect of the publication in a newspaper of a 
substantially true report of any proceedings of either House of Parliament or the 
Legislative Assembly, or, as the case may be, either House of the Legislature, 
of a State, unless the publication is proved to have been made with malice:
Provided that nothing in this clause shall apply to the publication of any 
report of the proceedings of a secret sitting of either House of Parliament or the 
Legislative Assembly, or, as the case may be, either House of the Legislature, 
of a State.
(2) Clause (1) shall apply in relation to reports or matters broadcast by 
means of wireless telegraphy as part of any programme or service provided by 
means of a broadcasting station as it applies in relation to reports or matters 
published in a newspaper.
Explanation.—In this article, “newspaper” includes a news agency report 
containing material for publication in a newspaper.]
2[361B. Disqualification for appointment on remunerative political 
post.—A member of a House belonging to any political party who is 
disqualified for being a member of the House under paragraph 2 of the Tenth 
Schedule shall also be disqualified to hold any remunerative political post for 
duration of the period commencing from  the date of his disqualification  till the 
date on which the term of his office as such member would expire or till the  
date on which he contests an election to a House and is declared  elected, 
whichever is earlier.
Explanation.— For the purposes of this article,—
(a)
the expression
“House”
has
the meaning assigned to it in 
clause (a) of paragraph 1 of the  Tenth Schedule;  
(b) the expression “remunerative political post” means any office—                 
(i) under  the Government of India or the Government of a 
State where the salary or remuneration   for  such office is paid 
out of the public revenue of the Government of India or the 
Government of the State, as the case may be; or  
______________________________________________
1.  Art. 361A ins.  by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 42
(w.e.f. 20-6-1979).
2. Art. 361B ins. by the Constitution (Ninety-first Amendment) Act, 2003, s. 4 
(w.e.f. 1-1-2004).

THE CONSTITUTION OF  INDIA
(Part XIX.—MISCELLANEOUS)
221
(ii) under a body, whether incorporated or not, which is 
wholly or partially owned by the Government of India or the 
Government of State, and the salary or remuneration for such 
office is paid by such body, 
except where such salary or remuneration paid is compensatory in nature.] 
362. [Rights and privileges of Rulers of Indian States.].—Omitted by the 
Constitution (Twenty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1971, s. 2 (w.e.f. 28-12-1971).
363. Bar to interference by courts in disputes arising out of certain 
treaties, agreements, etc.—(1) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution 
but subject to the provisions of article 143, neither the Supreme Court nor any 
other court shall have jurisdiction in any dispute arising out of any provision of 
a treaty, agreement, covenant, engagement, sanad or other similar instrument 
which was entered into or executed before the commencement of this 
Constitution by any Ruler of an Indian State and to which the Government of 
the Dominion of India or any of its predecessor Governments was a party and 
which has or has been continued in operation after such commencement, or in 
any dispute in respect of any right accruing under or any liability or obligation 
arising out of any of the provisions of this Constitution relating to any such 
treaty, agreement, covenant, engagement, sanad or other similar instrument.
(2) In this article—
(a) “Indian State” means any territory recognised before the 
commencement of this Constitution by His Majesty or the Government 
of the Dominion of India as being such a State; and
(b) “Ruler” includes the Prince, Chief or other person recognised 
before such commencement by His Majesty or the Government of the 
Dominion of India as the Ruler of any Indian State.
1[363A. Recognition granted to Rulers of Indian States to cease and 
privy purses to be abolished.—Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution 
or in any law for the time being in force—
(a) the Prince, Chief or other person who, at any time before 
the commencement of the Constitution (Twenty-sixth Amendment) 
Act, 1971, was recognised by the President as the Ruler of an Indian 
State or any person who, at any time before such commencement, was 
recognised by the President as the successor of such ruler shall, on and 
from such commencement, cease to be recognised as such Ruler or the 
successor of such Ruler;
______________________________________________
1. Art. 363A ins. by the Constitution (Twenty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1971, s. 3 
(w.e.f. 28-12-1971).

THE CONSTITUTION OF  INDIA
(Part XIX.—MISCELLANEOUS)
222
(b) on and from the commencement of the Constitution (Twenty-
sixth Amendment) Act, 1971, privy purse is abolished and all rights, 
liabilities and obligations in respect of privy purse are extinguished and 
accordingly the Ruler or, as the case may be, the successor of such 
Ruler, referred to in clause (a) or any other person shall not be paid any 
sum as privy purse.]
364. Special provisions as to major ports and aerodromes.—(1) 
Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, the President may by public 
notification direct that as from such date as may be specified in the 
notification— 
(a) any law made by Parliament or by the Legislature of a State 
shall not apply to any major port or aerodrome or shall apply thereto 
subject to such exceptions or modifications as may be specified in the 
notification; or 
(b) any existing law shall cease to have effect in any major port or 
aerodrome except as respects things done or omitted to be done before 
the said date, or shall in its application to such port or aerodrome have 
effect subject to such exceptions or modifications as may be specified in 
the notification.
(2) In this article—
(a) “major port” means a port declared to be a major port by or 
under any law made by Parliament or any existing law and includes all 
areas for the time being included within the limits of such port;
(b) “aerodrome” means aerodrome as defined for the purposes of 
the enactments relating to airways, aircraft and air navigation.
365. Effect of failure to comply with, or to give effect to, directions 
given by the Union.—Where any State has failed to comply with, or to give 
effect to, any directions given in the exercise of the executive power of the Union 
under any of the provisions of this Constitution, it shall be lawful for the 
President to hold that a situation has arisen in which the Government of the State 
cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of this Constitution.
366. Definitions.—In this Constitution, unless the context otherwise 
requires, the following expressions have the meanings hereby respectively 
assigned to them, that is to say—
(1) “agricultural income” means agricultural income as defined 
for the purposes of the enactments relating to Indian income-tax;

THE CONSTITUTION OF  INDIA
(Part XIX.—MISCELLANEOUS)
223
(2) “an Anglo-Indian” means a person whose father or any of 
whose other male progenitors in the male line is or was of European 
descent but who is domiciled within the territory of India and is or was 
born within such territory of parents habitually resident therein and not 
established there for temporary purposes only;
(3) “article” means an article of this Constitution; 
(4) “borrow” includes the raising of money by the grant of 
annuities, and “loan” shall be construed accordingly;
1[(4A)*                        *
*                         *] 
(5) “clause” means a clause of the article in which the expression 
occurs;
(6) “corporation tax” means any tax on income, so far as that tax 
is payable by companies and is a tax in the case of which the following 
conditions are fulfilled:—
(a) that it is not chargeable in respect of agricultural 
income; 
(b) that no deduction in respect of the tax paid by 
companies is, by any enactments which may apply to the tax, 
authorised to be made from dividends payable by the companies 
to individuals;
(c) that no provision exists for taking the tax so paid into 
account in computing for the purposes of Indian income-tax the 
total income of individuals receiving such dividends, or in 
computing the Indian income-tax payable by, or refundable to, 
such individuals;
(7) “corresponding Province”, “corresponding Indian State” or 
“corresponding State” means in cases of doubt such Province, Indian 
State or State as may be determined by the President to be the 
corresponding Province, the corresponding Indian State or the 
corresponding State, as the case may be, for the particular purpose in 
question;
______________________________________________
1. Cl. (4A) was ins. by the Constitution  (Forty-second Amendment)  Act, 1976, s. 54 
(w.e.f. 1-2-1977) and subsequently omitted by the Constitution (Forty-third Amendment)  
Act, 1977, s. 11 (w.e.f. 13-4-1978).

THE CONSTITUTION OF  INDIA
(Part XIX.—MISCELLANEOUS)
224
(8) “debt” includes any liability in respect of any obligation to 
repay capital sums by way of annuities and any liability under any 
guarantee, and “debt charges” shall be construed accordingly;
(9) “estate duty” means a duty to be assessed on or by reference to 
the principal value, ascertained in accordance with such rules as may be 
prescribed by or under laws made by Parliament or the Legislature of a 
State relating to the duty, of all property passing upon death or deemed, 
under the provisions of the said laws, so to pass;
(10) “existing law” means any law, Ordinance, order, bye-law, 
rule or regulation passed or made before the commencement of this 
Constitution by any Legislature, authority or person having power to 
make such a law, Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule or regulation; 
(11) “Federal Court” means the Federal Court constituted under 
the Government of India Act, 1935;
(12) “goods” includes all materials, commodities, and articles;
1[(12A) “goods and services tax” means any tax on supply of 
goods, or services or both except taxes on the supply of the alcoholic 
liquor for human consumption];
(13) “guarantee” includes any obligation undertaken before the 
commencement of this Constitution to make payments in the event of the 
profits of an undertaking falling short of a specified amount;
(14) “High Court” means any Court which is deemed for the 
purposes of this Constitution to be a High Court for any State and 
includes—
(a) any Court in the territory of India constituted or 
reconstituted under this Constitution as a High Court; and
(b) any other Court in the territory of India which may be 
declared by Parliament by law to be a High Court for all or any of 
the purposes of this Constitution;
(15) “Indian State” means any territory which the Government of 
the Dominion of India recognised as such a State;
______________________________________________
1. Ins. by the Constitution (One Hundred and First Amendment) Act, 2016, s. 14(i)
(w.e.f. 16-9-2016).

THE CONSTITUTION OF  INDIA
(Part XIX.—MISCELLANEOUS)
225
(16) “Part”  means a Part of this Constitution;
(17) “pension” means a pension, whether contributory or not, of 
any kind whatsoever payable to or in respect of any person, and includes 
retired pay so payable; a gratuity so payable and any sum or sums so 
payable by way of the return, with or without interest thereon or any

(19) “public notification” means a notification in the Gazette of

369. Temporary power to Parliament to make laws with respect to 
certain matters in the State List as if they were matters in the Concurrent 
List.—Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament shall, during 
a period of five years from the commencement of this Constitution, have power 
to make laws with respect to the following matters as if they were enumerated 
in the Concurrent List, namely:— 
(a) trade and commerce within a State in, and the production, supply 
and distribution of, cotton and woollen textiles, raw cotton (including 
ginned cotton and unginned cotton or kapas), cotton seed, paper 
(including newsprint), food-stuffs (including edible oilseeds and oil), 
cattle fodder (including oil-cakes and other concentrates), coal 
(including coke and derivatives of coal), iron, steel and mica;
(b) offences against laws with respect to any of the matters mentioned
in clause (a), jurisdiction and powers of all courts except the Supreme 
Court with respect to any of those matters, and fees in respect of any of 
those matters but not including fees taken in any court,
but any law made by Parliament, which Parliament would not but for the 
provisions of this article have been competent to make, shall, to the extent of the 
incompetency, cease to have effect on the expiration of the said period, except as 
respects things done or omitted to be done before the expiration thereof.

nodes.title: Protection of publication of proceedings of Parliament and State Legislatures.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines various provisions of the Constitution of India, specifically focusing on miscellaneous articles. Key points include:

1. **Protection of Parliamentary Proceedings (Article 361A)**: It provides immunity from legal proceedings for the publication of true reports of parliamentary proceedings, except in cases of malice or secret sittings.

2. **Disqualification for Political Posts (Article 361B)**: Members of a political party disqualified under the Tenth Schedule are also disqualified from holding remunerative political posts during their disqualification period.

3. **Judicial Limitations on Treaties (Article 363)**: It restricts the jurisdiction of courts in disputes arising from treaties or agreements made by rulers of Indian states before the Constitution came into effect.

4. **Abolition of Privy Purses (Article 363A)**: It states that recognition of rulers of Indian states ceases and privy purses are abolished.

5. **Special Provisions for Major Ports and Aerodromes (Article 364)**: The President can modify laws applicable to major ports and aerodromes through public notification.

6. **State Compliance with Union Directives (Article 365)**: It allows the President to determine if a state government cannot function according to the Constitution if it fails to comply with Union directives.

7. **Definitions (Article 366)**: It provides definitions for various terms used throughout the Constitution, including "agricultural income," "Indian State," and "Scheduled Castes."

8. **Amendment Procedures (Article 368)**: It outlines the process for amending the Constitution, requiring a two-thirds majority in both Houses of Parliament and, in some cases, ratification by state legislatures.

9. **Temporary and Special Provisions (Part XXI)**: This section includes provisions for specific states, such as Jammu and Kashmir, Nagaland, and others, detailing their unique governance and legislative frameworks.

10. **Continuance of Existing Laws (Article 372)**: It states that existing laws remain in force until amended or repealed by competent authorities.

Overall, the document emphasizes the legal framework governing parliamentary proceedings, disqualifications, state compliance, and special provisions for certain regions within India.

THE CONSTITUTION OF  INDIA
(Part XIX.—MISCELLANEOUS)
220
1[361A. Protection of publication of proceedings of Parliament and 
State Legislatures.—(1) No person shall be liable to any proceedings, civil or 
criminal, in any court in respect of the publication in a newspaper of a 
substantially true report of any proceedings of either House of Parliament or the 
Legislative Assembly, or, as the case may be, either House of the Legislature, 
of a State, unless the publication is proved to have been made with malice:
Provided that nothing in this clause shall apply to the publication of any 
report of the proceedings of a secret sitting of either House of Parliament or the 
Legislative Assembly, or, as the case may be, either House of the Legislature, 
of a State.
(2) Clause (1) shall apply in relation to reports or matters broadcast by 
means of wireless telegraphy as part of any programme or service provided by 
means of a broadcasting station as it applies in relation to reports or matters 
published in a newspaper.
Explanation.—In this article, “newspaper” includes a news agency report 
containing material for publication in a newspaper.]
2[361B. Disqualification for appointment on remunerative political 
post.—A member of a House belonging to any political party who is 
disqualified for being a member of the House under paragraph 2 of the Tenth 
Schedule shall also be disqualified to hold any remunerative political post for 
duration of the period commencing from  the date of his disqualification  till the 
date on which the term of his office as such member would expire or till the  
date on which he contests an election to a House and is declared  elected, 
whichever is earlier.
Explanation.— For the purposes of this article,—
(a)
the expression
“House”
has
the meaning assigned to it in 
clause (a) of paragraph 1 of the  Tenth Schedule;  
(b) the expression “remunerative political post” means any office—                 
(i) under  the Government of India or the Government of a 
State where the salary or remuneration   for  such office is paid 
out of the public revenue of the Government of India or the 
Government of the State, as the case may be; or  
______________________________________________
1.  Art. 361A ins.  by the Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, s. 42
(w.e.f. 20-6-1979).
2. Art. 361B ins. by the Constitution (Ninety-first Amendment) Act, 2003, s. 4 
(w.e.f. 1-1-2004).

THE CONSTITUTION OF  INDIA
(Part XIX.—MISCELLANEOUS)
221
(ii) under a body, whether incorporated or not, which is 
wholly or partially owned by the Government of India or the 
Government of State, and the salary or remuneration for such 
office is paid by such body, 
except where such salary or remuneration paid is compensatory in nature.] 
362. [Rights and privileges of Rulers of Indian States.].—Omitted by the 
Constitution (Twenty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1971, s. 2 (w.e.f. 28-12-1971).
363. Bar to interference by courts in disputes arising out of certain 
treaties, agreements, etc.—(1) Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution 
but subject to the provisions of article 143, neither the Supreme Court nor any 
other court shall have jurisdiction in any dispute arising out of any provision of 
a treaty, agreement, covenant, engagement, sanad or other similar instrument 
which was entered into or executed before the commencement of this 
Constitution by any Ruler of an Indian State and to which the Government of 
the Dominion of India or any of its predecessor Governments was a party and 
which has or has been continued in operation after such commencement, or in 
any dispute in respect of any right accruing under or any liability or obligation 
arising out of any of the provisions of this Constitution relating to any such 
treaty, agreement, covenant, engagement, sanad or other similar instrument.
(2) In this article—
(a) “Indian State” means any territory recognised before the 
commencement of this Constitution by His Majesty or the Government 
of the Dominion of India as being such a State; and
(b) “Ruler” includes the Prince, Chief or other person recognised 
before such commencement by His Majesty or the Government of the 
Dominion of India as the Ruler of any Indian State.
1[363A. Recognition granted to Rulers of Indian States to cease and 
privy purses to be abolished.—Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution 
or in any law for the time being in force—
(a) the Prince, Chief or other person who, at any time before 
the commencement of the Constitution (Twenty-sixth Amendment) 
Act, 1971, was recognised by the President as the Ruler of an Indian 
State or any person who, at any time before such commencement, was 
recognised by the President as the successor of such ruler shall, on and 
from such commencement, cease to be recognised as such Ruler or the 
successor of such Ruler;
______________________________________________
1. Art. 363A ins. by the Constitution (Twenty-sixth Amendment) Act, 1971, s. 3 
(w.e.f. 28-12-1971).

THE CONSTITUTION OF  INDIA
(Part XIX.—MISCELLANEOUS)
222
(b) on and from the commencement of the Constitution (Twenty-
sixth Amendment) Act, 1971, privy purse is abolished and all rights, 
liabilities and obligations in respect of privy purse are extinguished and 
accordingly the Ruler or, as the case may be, the successor of such 
Ruler, referred to in clause (a) or any other person shall not be paid any 
sum as privy purse.]
364. Special provisions as to major ports and aerodromes.—(1) 
Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, the President may by public 
notification direct that as from such date as may be specified in the 
notification— 
(a) any law made by Parliament or by the Legislature of a State 
shall not apply to any major port or aerodrome or shall apply thereto 
subject to such exceptions or modifications as may be specified in the 
notification; or 
(b) any existing law shall cease to have effect in any major port or 
aerodrome except as respects things done or omitted to be done before 
the said date, or shall in its application to such port or aerodrome have 
effect subject to such exceptions or modifications as may be specified in 
the notification.
(2) In this article—
(a) “major port” means a port declared to be a major port by or 
under any law made by Parliament or any existing law and includes all 
areas for the time being included within the limits of such port;
(b) “aerodrome” means aerodrome as defined for the purposes of 
the enactments relating to airways, aircraft and air navigation.
365. Effect of failure to comply with, or to give effect to, directions 
given by the Union.—Where any State has failed to comply with, or to give 
effect to, any directions given in the exercise of the executive power of the Union 
under any of the provisions of this Constitution, it shall be lawful for the 
President to hold that a situation has arisen in which the Government of the State 
cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of this Constitution.
366. Definitions.—In this Constitution, unless the context otherwise 
requires, the following expressions have the meanings hereby respectively 
assigned to them, that is to say—
(1) “agricultural income” means agricultural income as defined 
for the purposes of the enactments relating to Indian income-tax;

(Part XIX.—MISCELLANEOUS)

whose other male progenitors in the male line is or was of European

(3) “article” means an article of this Constitution;

369. Temporary power to Parliament to make laws with respect to 
certain matters in the State List as if they were matters in the Concurrent 
List.—Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, Parliament shall, during 
a period of five years from the commencement of this Constitution, have power 
to make laws with respect to the following matters as if they were enumerated 
in the Concurrent List, namely:— 
(a) trade and commerce within a State in, and the production, supply 
and distribution of, cotton and woollen textiles, raw cotton (including 
ginned cotton and unginned cotton or kapas), cotton seed, paper 
(including newsprint), food-stuffs (including edible oilseeds and oil), 
cattle fodder (including oil-cakes and other concentrates), coal 
(including coke and derivatives of coal), iron, steel and mica;
(b) offences against laws with respect to any of the matters mentioned
in clause (a), jurisdiction and powers of all courts except the Supreme 
Court with respect to any of those matters, and fees in respect of any of 
those matters but not including fees taken in any court,
but any law made by Parliament, which Parliament would not but for the 
provisions of this article have been competent to make, shall, to the extent of the 
incompetency, cease to have effect on the expiration of the said period, except as 
respects things done or omitted to be done before the expiration thereof.

Provided that no such order shall be made after the first meeting of 
Parliament duly constituted under Chapter II of Part V.
(2) Every order made under clause (1) shall be laid before Parliament.
(3) The powers conferred on the President by this article, by article 324, by 
clause (3) of article 367 and by article 391 shall, before the commencement of this 
Constitution, be exercisable by the Governor-General of the Dominion of India.

252
PART XXII
SHORT TITLE, COMMENCEMENT, 1[AUTHORITATIVE 
TEXT IN HINDI] AND REPEALS
393. Short title.—This Constitution may be called the Constitution of 
India. 
394.  Commencement.—This article and articles 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60,  324, 
366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392 and 393 shall come into force at once, and 
the remaining provisions of this Constitution shall come into force on the 
twenty-sixth day of January, 1950, which day is referred to in this Constitution 
as the commencement of this Constitution. 
2[394A. Authoritative text in the Hindi language.—(1) The President 
shall cause to be published under his authority,— 
(a) the translation of this Constitution in the Hindi language, 
signed by the members of the Constituent Assembly, with such 
modifications as may be necessary to bring it in conformity with the 
language, style and terminology adopted in the authoritative texts of 
Central Acts in the Hindi language, and incorporating therein all the 
amendments of this Constitution made before such publication; and
(b) the translation in the Hindi language of every amendment of 
this Constitution made in the English language. 
(2) The translation of this Constitution and of every amendment thereof 
published under clause (1) shall be construed to have the same meaning as  the 
original thereof and if any difficulty arises in so construing any part of such 
translation, the President shall cause the same to be revised suitably.
(3) The translation of this Constitution and of every amendment thereof 
published under this article shall  be deemed to be, for all purposes, the 
authoritative text thereof in the Hindi language.]
395. Repeals.—
The Indian Independence Act, 1947, and the 
Government of India Act, 1935, together with all enactments amending or 
supplementing the latter Act, but not including the Abolition of Privy Council 
Jurisdiction Act, 1949, are hereby repealed.

364. Special provisions as to major ports and aerodromes.—(1) 
Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, the President may by public 
notification direct that as from such date as may be specified in the 
notification— 
(a) any law made by Parliament or by the Legislature of a State 
shall not apply to any major port or aerodrome or shall apply thereto 
subject to such exceptions or modifications as may be specified in the 
notification; or 
(b) any existing law shall cease to have effect in any major port or 
aerodrome except as respects things done or omitted to be done before 
the said date, or shall in its application to such port or aerodrome have 
effect subject to such exceptions or modifications as may be specified in 
the notification.
(2) In this article—
(a) “major port” means a port declared to be a major port by or 
under any law made by Parliament or any existing law and includes all 
areas for the time being included within the limits of such port;
(b) “aerodrome” means aerodrome as defined for the purposes of 
the enactments relating to airways, aircraft and air navigation.
365. Effect of failure to comply with, or to give effect to, directions 
given by the Union.—Where any State has failed to comply with, or to give 
effect to, any directions given in the exercise of the executive power of the Union 
under any of the provisions of this Constitution, it shall be lawful for the 
President to hold that a situation has arisen in which the Government of the State 
cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of this Constitution.
366. Definitions.—In this Constitution, unless the context otherwise 
requires, the following expressions have the meanings hereby respectively 
assigned to them, that is to say—
(1) “agricultural income” means agricultural income as defined

(Part XXI.—Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions)
247
Explanation I.—The expression “law in force” in this article shall 
include a law passed or made by a Legislature or other competent authority in 
the territory of India before the commencement of this Constitution and not 
previously repealed, notwithstanding that it or parts of it may not be then in 
operation either at all or in particular areas.
Explanation II.—Any law passed or made by a Legislature or other 
competent authority in the territory of India which immediately before the 
commencement of this Constitution had extra-territorial effect as well as effect 
in the territory of India shall, subject to any such adaptations and modifications 
as aforesaid, continue to have such extra-territorial effect.
Explanation III.—Nothing in this article shall be construed as continuing 
any temporary law in force beyond the date fixed for its expiration or the date 
on which it would have expired if this Constitution had  not come into force.
Explanation IV.—An Ordinance promulgated by the Governor of a 
Province under section 88 of the Government of India Act, 1935, and in force 
immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall, unless 
withdrawn by the Governor of the corresponding State earlier, cease to operate 
at the expiration of six weeks from the first meeting after such commencement 
of the Legislative Assembly of that State functioning under clause (1) of article 
382, and  nothing in this article shall be construed as continuing any such 
Ordinance in force beyond the said period.
1[372A.  Power of the President to adapt laws.—(1) For the purposes 
of bringing the provisions of any law in force in India or in any part thereof, 
immediately before the commencement of the Constitution (Seventh 
Amendment) Act, 1956, into accord with the provisions of this Constitution as 
amended by that Act, the President may by order made before the first day of 
November, 1957, make such adaptations and modifications of the law, whether 
by way of repeal or amendment, as may be necessary or expedient, and provide 
that the law shall, as from such date as may be  specified in the order, have 
effect subject to the adaptations and modifications so made, and any such 
adaptation or modification shall not be questioned in any court of law.
(2) Nothing in clause (1) shall be deemed to  prevent a competent 
Legislature or other competent authority from repealing or amending any law 
adapted or modified by the President  under the said clause.]

(Part XXI.—Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions)
248
373. Power of President to make order in respect of persons under 
preventive detention in certain cases.—Until provision is made by Parliament 
under clause (7) of article 22, or until the expiration of one year from the 
commencement of this Constitution, whichever  is earlier, the said  article shall 
have effect as if for any reference to Parliament in clauses (4) and (7) thereof 
there were substituted a reference to the President and for any reference to any 
law made by Parliament in those clauses there were substituted a reference to 
an order made by the President.
374. Provisions as to Judges of the Federal Court and proceedings 
pending in the Federal Court or before His Majesty in Council.—(1) The 
Judges of the Federal Court holding office immediately before the 
commencement of this Constitution shall, unless they have elected otherwise, 
become on such commencement the Judges of the Supreme Court and shall 
thereupon be entitled to such salaries and allowances and to such rights in 
respect of leave of absence and pension as are provided for under article 125 in 
respect of the Judges of the Supreme Court.
(2) All suits, appeals and proceedings, civil or criminal, pending in the 
Federal Court at the commencement of this Constitution shall stand removed to 
the Supreme Court, and the Supreme Court shall have jurisdiction to hear and 
determine the same, and the judgments and  orders of the Federal Court delivered 
or made before the  commencement of this Constitution shall have the same force 
and effect as if they had been delivered or made by the Supreme Court.
(3) Nothing in this Constitution shall operate to invalidate the exercise of 
jurisdiction by His Majesty in Council to dispose of appeals and petitions from, 
or in respect of, any judgment, decree or order of any court within the territory 
of India in so far as the exercise of such jurisdiction is authorised by law, and 
any order of His Majesty in Council made on any such appeal or petition after 
the commencement of this Constitution shall for all purposes have effect as if it 
were an order or decree made by the Supreme Court in the exercise of the  
jurisdiction conferred on such Court by this Constitution.
(4) On and from the commencement of this Constitution the jurisdiction of 
the authority functioning as the Privy Council in a State specified in Part B of the 
First Schedule to entertain and dispose of appeals and petitions from or in respect 
of any judgment, decree or order of any court within that State shall cease, and all 
appeals and other proceedings pending before the said authority at such 
commencement shall be transferred to, and disposed of by, the Supreme Court.
(5) Further provision may be made by Parliament by law to give effect to 
the provisions of this article.

THE CONSTITUTION OF  INDIA
(Part XXI.—Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions)
249
375. Courts, authorities and officers to continue to function subject 
to the provisions of the Constitution.—All courts of civil, criminal and 
revenue jurisdiction, all authorities and all officers, judicial, executive and 
ministerial, throughout the territory of India, shall continue to exercise their 
respective functions subject to the provisions of this Constitution.
376. Provisions as to Judges of High Courts.—(1) Notwithstanding 
anything in clause (2) of article 217, the Judges of a High Court in any 
Province holding office immediately before the commencement of this 
Constitution shall, unless they have elected otherwise, become on such 
commencement the Judges of the High Court in the corresponding State, and 
shall thereupon be entitled to such salaries and allowances and to such rights in  
respect of leave of absence and pension as are provided for under article 221 in 
respect of the Judges of such High Court. 1[Any such Judge shall, 
notwithstanding that he is not a citizen of India, be eligible for appointment as 
Chief Justice of such High Court, or as Chief Justice or other Judge of any 
other High Court.] 
(2) The Judges of a High Court in any Indian State corresponding to any 
State specified in Part B of the First Schedule holding office immediately 
before the commencement of this Constitution shall, unless they have elected 
otherwise, become on such commencement the Judges of the High Court in the 
State so specified and shall, notwithstanding anything in clauses  (1) and (2) of 
article 217 but subject to the proviso to clause (1) of that article, continue to hold 
office until the expiration of such period as the President may by order determine. 
(3)  In this article, the expression “Judge” does not include an acting Judge 
or an additional Judge.
377. Provisions as to Comptroller and Auditor-General of India.—The 
Auditor-General of India holding office immediately before the commencement of 
this Constitution shall, unless  he has elected otherwise, become on such 
commencement the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India and shall thereupon 
be entitled to such salaries and to such rights in respect of leave of absence and 
pension as are provided for under clause (3) of article 148 in respect of the 
Comptroller and Auditor-General of India and be entitled to continue to hold office 
until the expiration of his term of office as determined under the provisions which 
were applicable to him immediately before such commencement.

378. Provisions as to Public Service Commissions.—(1) The members 
of the Public Service Commission for the Dominion of India holding office

(2) The Members of a Public Service Commission of a Province or of a

office immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall, unless they 
have elected otherwise, become on such commencement the members of the Public 
Service Commission for the corresponding State or the members of the Joint State

case may be, and shall, notwithstanding anything in clauses (1) and (2) of article 
316 but subject to the proviso to clause (2) of that article, continue to hold office 
until the expiration of their term of office as determined under the rules which  were 
applicable immediately before such commencement to such members.
1[378A. Special provision as to duration of Andhra Pradesh

(Part XXI.—Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions)

392. Power of the President to remove difficulties.—(1) The President 
may, for the purpose of removing any difficulties, particularly in relation to the 
transition from the provisions of the Government of India Act, 1935, to the 
provisions of this Constitution, by order direct that this Constitution shall, 
during such period as may be specified in the order, have effect subject to such 
adaptations, whether by way of modification, addition or omission, as he may 
deem to be necessary or expedient:
Provided that no such order shall be made after the first meeting of 
Parliament duly constituted under Chapter II of Part V.
(2) Every order made under clause (1) shall be laid before Parliament.
(3) The powers conferred on the President by this article, by article 324, by 
clause (3) of article 367 and by article 391 shall, before the commencement of this 
Constitution, be exercisable by the Governor-General of the Dominion of India.

PART XXII
SHORT TITLE, COMMENCEMENT, 1[AUTHORITATIVE 
TEXT IN HINDI] AND REPEALS
393. Short title.—This Constitution may be called the Constitution of 
India. 
394.  Commencement.—This article and articles 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60,  324, 
366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392 and 393 shall come into force at once, and 
the remaining provisions of this Constitution shall come into force on the 
twenty-sixth day of January, 1950, which day is referred to in this Constitution 
as the commencement of this Constitution. 
2[394A. Authoritative text in the Hindi language.—(1) The President 
shall cause to be published under his authority,— 
(a) the translation of this Constitution in the Hindi language, 
signed by the members of the Constituent Assembly, with such 
modifications as may be necessary to bring it in conformity with the 
language, style and terminology adopted in the authoritative texts of 
Central Acts in the Hindi language, and incorporating therein all the 
amendments of this Constitution made before such publication; and
(b) the translation in the Hindi language of every amendment of 
this Constitution made in the English language. 
(2) The translation of this Constitution and of every amendment thereof 
published under clause (1) shall be construed to have the same meaning as  the 
original thereof and if any difficulty arises in so construing any part of such 
translation, the President shall cause the same to be revised suitably.
(3) The translation of this Constitution and of every amendment thereof 
published under this article shall  be deemed to be, for all purposes, the 
authoritative text thereof in the Hindi language.]
395. Repeals.—
The Indian Independence Act, 1947, and the 
Government of India Act, 1935, together with all enactments amending or 
supplementing the latter Act, but not including the Abolition of Privy Council 
Jurisdiction Act, 1949, are hereby repealed.

nodes.title: Rights and privileges of Rulers of Indian States.
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines various provisions of the Constitution of India, specifically focusing on miscellaneous aspects. Key points include the abolition of the privy purse as per the Twenty-sixth Amendment Act of 1971, which extinguishes all rights related to it. It also details the President's authority to modify the application of laws concerning major ports and aerodromes, including the definitions of these terms. Additionally, it addresses the consequences of a state's failure to comply with directions from the Union, allowing the President to determine if the state government can function according to constitutional provisions. The document further provides definitions for terms such as "agricultural income," "Anglo-Indian," and "corporation tax," clarifying their meanings within the context of the Constitution.
nodes.text:
THE CONSTITUTION OF  INDIA
(Part XIX.—MISCELLANEOUS)
222
(b) on and from the commencement of the Constitution (Twenty-
sixth Amendment) Act, 1971, privy purse is abolished and all rights, 
liabilities and obligations in respect of privy purse are extinguished and 
accordingly the Ruler or, as the case may be, the successor of such 
Ruler, referred to in clause (a) or any other person shall not be paid any 
sum as privy purse.]
364. Special provisions as to major ports and aerodromes.—(1) 
Notwithstanding anything in this Constitution, the President may by public 
notification direct that as from such date as may be specified in the 
notification— 
(a) any law made by Parliament or by the Legislature of a State 
shall not apply to any major port or aerodrome or shall apply thereto 
subject to such exceptions or modifications as may be specified in the 
notification; or 
(b) any existing law shall cease to have effect in any major port or 
aerodrome except as respects things done or omitted to be done before 
the said date, or shall in its application to such port or aerodrome have 
effect subject to such exceptions or modifications as may be specified in 
the notification.
(2) In this article—
(a) “major port” means a port declared to be a major port by or 
under any law made by Parliament or any existing law and includes all 
areas for the time being included within the limits of such port;
(b) “aerodrome” means aerodrome as defined for the purposes of 
the enactments relating to airways, aircraft and air navigation.
365. Effect of failure to comply with, or to give effect to, directions 
given by the Union.—Where any State has failed to comply with, or to give 
effect to, any directions given in the exercise of the executive power of the Union 
under any of the provisions of this Constitution, it shall be lawful for the 
President to hold that a situation has arisen in which the Government of the State 
cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of this Constitution.
366. Definitions.—In this Constitution, unless the context otherwise 
requires, the following expressions have the meanings hereby respectively 
assigned to them, that is to say—
(1) “agricultural income” means agricultural income as defined 
for the purposes of the enactments relating to Indian income-tax;

THE CONSTITUTION OF  INDIA
(Part XIX.—MISCELLANEOUS)
223
(2) “an Anglo-Indian” means a person whose father or any of 
whose other male progenitors in the male line is or was of European 
descent but who is domiciled within the territory of India and is or was 
born within such territory of parents habitually resident therein and not 
established there for temporary purposes only;
(3) “article” means an article of this Constitution; 
(4) “borrow” includes the raising of money by the grant of 
annuities, and “loan” shall be construed accordingly;
1[(4A)*                        *
*                         *] 
(5) “clause” means a clause of the article in which the expression 
occurs;
(6) “corporation tax” means any tax on income, so far as that tax 
is payable by companies and is a tax in the case of which the following 
conditions are fulfilled:—
(a) that it is not chargeable in respect of agricultural 
income; 
(b) that no deduction in respect of the tax paid by 
companies is, by any enactments which may apply to the tax, 
authorised to be made from dividends payable by the companies 
to individuals;
(c) that no provision exists for taking the tax so paid into 
account in computing for the purposes of Indian income-tax the 
total income of individuals receiving such dividends, or in 
computing the Indian income-tax payable by, or refundable to, 
such individuals;
(7) “corresponding Province”, “corresponding Indian State” or 
“corresponding State” means in cases of doubt such Province, Indian 
State or State as may be determined by the President to be the 
corresponding Province, the corresponding Indian State or the 
corresponding State, as the case may be, for the particular purpose in 
question;

Act, 1977, s. 11 (w.e.f. 13-4-1978).
