nodes.summary: The partial document discusses provisions related to the adaptation and continuation of existing laws in India following the enactment of the Constitution. It outlines the identification and reservation of posts for individuals from the Hyderabad-Karnataka region. It specifies that laws in force before the Constitution's commencement will remain effective until altered or repealed by competent authorities. The President is granted the power to adapt and modify these laws to align them with the Constitution, with certain limitations on the duration of this power. The document also clarifies the definitions of "law in force" and addresses the continuation of laws with extra-territorial effects, as well as the expiration of temporary laws and ordinances.

372. Continuance in force of existing laws and their adaptation.—(1) 
Notwithstanding the repeal by this Constitution of the enactments referred to in 
article 395 but subject to the other provisions of this Constitution, all the law in 
force in the territory of India immediately before the commencement of this 
Constitution shall continue in force therein until altered or repealed or amended 
by a competent Legislature or other competent authority.
(2) For the purpose of bringing the provisions of any law in force in the 
territory of India into accord with the provisions of this Constitution, the 
President may by order make such adaptations and modifications of such law, 
whether by way of repeal or amendment, as may be necessary or expedient, and 
provide that the law shall, as from such date as may be specified in the order, 
have effect subject to the adaptations and modifications so made, and any such 
adaptation or modification shall not be questioned in any court of law.

(a) to empower the President to make any adaptation or 
modification of any law after the expiration of 1[three years] from the 
commencement of this Constitution; or

authority from repealing or amending any law adapted or modified by 
the President under the said clause.

nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines various temporary, transitional, and special provisions of the Constitution of India, particularly focusing on the legal framework and the continuity of laws and judicial authorities following the Constitution's commencement. Key points include:

1. **Definition of "Law in Force"**: It clarifies that existing laws prior to the Constitution's commencement remain valid unless repealed, even if not operational in certain areas.

2. **Presidential Powers**: The President is granted the authority to adapt existing laws to align with the Constitution, with adaptations not subject to judicial review.

3. **Judicial Continuity**: Judges of the Federal Court and High Courts automatically transition to their respective roles in the Supreme Court and corresponding State High Courts, retaining their rights and benefits.

4. **Pending Proceedings**: All legal proceedings pending in the Federal Court are transferred to the Supreme Court, which assumes jurisdiction over them.

5. **Functioning of Courts and Authorities**: All existing courts and authorities continue to operate under the new constitutional framework.

6. **Public Service Commissions**: Members of existing Public Service Commissions transition to their roles under the new Constitution, maintaining their terms.

7. **Special Provisions for Andhra Pradesh**: Specific provisions regarding the duration of the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly are included.

8. **Repeals and Commencement**: The document specifies the short title of the Constitution, its commencement date, and repeals previous acts, including the Indian Independence Act and the Government of India Act.

Overall, the document emphasizes the transition from previous legal frameworks to the new constitutional order while ensuring continuity in governance and judicial processes.

Explanation I.—The expression “law in force” in this article shall 
include a law passed or made by a Legislature or other competent authority in

(Part XXI.—Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions)

373. Power of President to make order in respect of persons under 
preventive detention in certain cases.—Until provision is made by Parliament 
under clause (7) of article 22, or until the expiration of one year from the 
commencement of this Constitution, whichever  is earlier, the said  article shall 
have effect as if for any reference to Parliament in clauses (4) and (7) thereof 
there were substituted a reference to the President and for any reference to any 
law made by Parliament in those clauses there were substituted a reference to 
an order made by the President.
374. Provisions as to Judges of the Federal Court and proceedings 
pending in the Federal Court or before His Majesty in Council.—(1) The 
Judges of the Federal Court holding office immediately before the 
commencement of this Constitution shall, unless they have elected otherwise, 
become on such commencement the Judges of the Supreme Court and shall 
thereupon be entitled to such salaries and allowances and to such rights in 
respect of leave of absence and pension as are provided for under article 125 in 
respect of the Judges of the Supreme Court.
(2) All suits, appeals and proceedings, civil or criminal, pending in the 
Federal Court at the commencement of this Constitution shall stand removed to 
the Supreme Court, and the Supreme Court shall have jurisdiction to hear and 
determine the same, and the judgments and  orders of the Federal Court delivered 
or made before the  commencement of this Constitution shall have the same force 
and effect as if they had been delivered or made by the Supreme Court.
(3) Nothing in this Constitution shall operate to invalidate the exercise of 
jurisdiction by His Majesty in Council to dispose of appeals and petitions from, 
or in respect of, any judgment, decree or order of any court within the territory 
of India in so far as the exercise of such jurisdiction is authorised by law, and 
any order of His Majesty in Council made on any such appeal or petition after 
the commencement of this Constitution shall for all purposes have effect as if it 
were an order or decree made by the Supreme Court in the exercise of the  
jurisdiction conferred on such Court by this Constitution.
(4) On and from the commencement of this Constitution the jurisdiction of 
the authority functioning as the Privy Council in a State specified in Part B of the 
First Schedule to entertain and dispose of appeals and petitions from or in respect 
of any judgment, decree or order of any court within that State shall cease, and all 
appeals and other proceedings pending before the said authority at such 
commencement shall be transferred to, and disposed of by, the Supreme Court.
(5) Further provision may be made by Parliament by law to give effect to 
the provisions of this article.

THE CONSTITUTION OF  INDIA
(Part XXI.—Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions)
249
375. Courts, authorities and officers to continue to function subject 
to the provisions of the Constitution.—All courts of civil, criminal and 
revenue jurisdiction, all authorities and all officers, judicial, executive and 
ministerial, throughout the territory of India, shall continue to exercise their 
respective functions subject to the provisions of this Constitution.
376. Provisions as to Judges of High Courts.—(1) Notwithstanding 
anything in clause (2) of article 217, the Judges of a High Court in any 
Province holding office immediately before the commencement of this 
Constitution shall, unless they have elected otherwise, become on such 
commencement the Judges of the High Court in the corresponding State, and 
shall thereupon be entitled to such salaries and allowances and to such rights in  
respect of leave of absence and pension as are provided for under article 221 in 
respect of the Judges of such High Court. 1[Any such Judge shall, 
notwithstanding that he is not a citizen of India, be eligible for appointment as 
Chief Justice of such High Court, or as Chief Justice or other Judge of any 
other High Court.] 
(2) The Judges of a High Court in any Indian State corresponding to any 
State specified in Part B of the First Schedule holding office immediately 
before the commencement of this Constitution shall, unless they have elected 
otherwise, become on such commencement the Judges of the High Court in the 
State so specified and shall, notwithstanding anything in clauses  (1) and (2) of 
article 217 but subject to the proviso to clause (1) of that article, continue to hold 
office until the expiration of such period as the President may by order determine. 
(3)  In this article, the expression “Judge” does not include an acting Judge 
or an additional Judge.
377. Provisions as to Comptroller and Auditor-General of India.—The 
Auditor-General of India holding office immediately before the commencement of 
this Constitution shall, unless  he has elected otherwise, become on such 
commencement the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India and shall thereupon 
be entitled to such salaries and to such rights in respect of leave of absence and 
pension as are provided for under clause (3) of article 148 in respect of the 
Comptroller and Auditor-General of India and be entitled to continue to hold office 
until the expiration of his term of office as determined under the provisions which 
were applicable to him immediately before such commencement.
______________________________________________

(Part XXI.—Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions)

may, for the purpose of removing any difficulties, particularly in relation to the

during such period as may be specified in the order, have effect subject to such

PART XXII
SHORT TITLE, COMMENCEMENT, 1[AUTHORITATIVE 
TEXT IN HINDI] AND REPEALS
393. Short title.—This Constitution may be called the Constitution of 
India. 
394.  Commencement.—This article and articles 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60,  324, 
366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392 and 393 shall come into force at once, and 
the remaining provisions of this Constitution shall come into force on the 
twenty-sixth day of January, 1950, which day is referred to in this Constitution 
as the commencement of this Constitution. 
2[394A. Authoritative text in the Hindi language.—(1) The President 
shall cause to be published under his authority,— 
(a) the translation of this Constitution in the Hindi language, 
signed by the members of the Constituent Assembly, with such 
modifications as may be necessary to bring it in conformity with the 
language, style and terminology adopted in the authoritative texts of

amendments of this Constitution made before such publication; and
(b) the translation in the Hindi language of every amendment of 
this Constitution made in the English language. 
(2) The translation of this Constitution and of every amendment thereof 
published under clause (1) shall be construed to have the same meaning as  the 
original thereof and if any difficulty arises in so construing any part of such 
translation, the President shall cause the same to be revised suitably.

published under this article shall  be deemed to be, for all purposes, the 
authoritative text thereof in the Hindi language.]

Government of India Act, 1935, together with all enactments amending or

nodes.summary: The partial document outlines temporary and transitional provisions in the Constitution of India, specifically focusing on the powers of Parliament regarding certain matters in the State List and special provisions for the State of Jammu and Kashmir. It details the temporary authority granted to Parliament to legislate on specific subjects as if they were in the Concurrent List for a period of five years from the Constitution's commencement. These subjects include trade, commerce, and various commodities such as textiles, foodstuffs, and minerals. Additionally, it discusses the limitations on Parliament's power to legislate for Jammu and Kashmir, emphasizing that such powers are contingent upon the President's declaration in consultation with the State Government. The document also references the modification of Article 370, which previously granted special status to Jammu and Kashmir, indicating that most provisions of the Constitution now apply to the state without exceptions.

374. Provisions as to Judges of the Federal Court and proceedings 
pending in the Federal Court or before His Majesty in Council.—(1) The 
Judges of the Federal Court holding office immediately before the 
commencement of this Constitution shall, unless they have elected otherwise, 
become on such commencement the Judges of the Supreme Court and shall 
thereupon be entitled to such salaries and allowances and to such rights in 
respect of leave of absence and pension as are provided for under article 125 in 
respect of the Judges of the Supreme Court.
(2) All suits, appeals and proceedings, civil or criminal, pending in the 
Federal Court at the commencement of this Constitution shall stand removed to 
the Supreme Court, and the Supreme Court shall have jurisdiction to hear and 
determine the same, and the judgments and  orders of the Federal Court delivered 
or made before the  commencement of this Constitution shall have the same force 
and effect as if they had been delivered or made by the Supreme Court.
(3) Nothing in this Constitution shall operate to invalidate the exercise of 
jurisdiction by His Majesty in Council to dispose of appeals and petitions from, 
or in respect of, any judgment, decree or order of any court within the territory 
of India in so far as the exercise of such jurisdiction is authorised by law, and 
any order of His Majesty in Council made on any such appeal or petition after 
the commencement of this Constitution shall for all purposes have effect as if it 
were an order or decree made by the Supreme Court in the exercise of the  
jurisdiction conferred on such Court by this Constitution.
(4) On and from the commencement of this Constitution the jurisdiction of 
the authority functioning as the Privy Council in a State specified in Part B of the 
First Schedule to entertain and dispose of appeals and petitions from or in respect 
of any judgment, decree or order of any court within that State shall cease, and all 
appeals and other proceedings pending before the said authority at such 
commencement shall be transferred to, and disposed of by, the Supreme Court.
(5) Further provision may be made by Parliament by law to give effect to 
the provisions of this article.

Comptroller and Auditor-General of India and be entitled to continue to hold office

393. Short title.—This Constitution may be called the Constitution of 
India. 
394.  Commencement.—This article and articles 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60,  324, 
366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392 and 393 shall come into force at once, and 
the remaining provisions of this Constitution shall come into force on the 
twenty-sixth day of January, 1950, which day is referred to in this Constitution 
as the commencement of this Constitution. 
2[394A. Authoritative text in the Hindi language.—(1) The President 
shall cause to be published under his authority,— 
(a) the translation of this Constitution in the Hindi language, 
signed by the members of the Constituent Assembly, with such 
modifications as may be necessary to bring it in conformity with the 
language, style and terminology adopted in the authoritative texts of 
Central Acts in the Hindi language, and incorporating therein all the 
amendments of this Constitution made before such publication; and
(b) the translation in the Hindi language of every amendment of 
this Constitution made in the English language. 
(2) The translation of this Constitution and of every amendment thereof 
published under clause (1) shall be construed to have the same meaning as  the 
original thereof and if any difficulty arises in so construing any part of such 
translation, the President shall cause the same to be revised suitably.
(3) The translation of this Constitution and of every amendment thereof 
published under this article shall  be deemed to be, for all purposes, the 
authoritative text thereof in the Hindi language.]
395. Repeals.—
The Indian Independence Act, 1947, and the 
Government of India Act, 1935, together with all enactments amending or 
supplementing the latter Act, but not including the Abolition of Privy Council 
Jurisdiction Act, 1949, are hereby repealed.

nodes.title: SHORT TITLE, COMMENCEMENT, AUTHORITATIVE TEXT IN HINDI AND REPEALS
Short title.
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines key provisions related to the Constitution of India, including its short title, commencement, and the establishment of an authoritative Hindi text. It specifies that the Constitution may be referred to as the "Constitution of India" and details the articles that came into force immediately versus those that took effect on January 26, 1950. Additionally, it mandates the publication of a Hindi translation of the Constitution and its amendments, ensuring that this translation holds the same authoritative status as the original English text. Finally, it includes a repeal of previous legislative acts, specifically the Indian Independence Act of 1947 and the Government of India Act of 1935, while excluding the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act of 1949.
nodes.text:
252
PART XXII
SHORT TITLE, COMMENCEMENT, 1[AUTHORITATIVE 
TEXT IN HINDI] AND REPEALS
393. Short title.—This Constitution may be called the Constitution of 
India. 
394.  Commencement.—This article and articles 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 60,  324, 
366, 367, 379, 380, 388, 391, 392 and 393 shall come into force at once, and 
the remaining provisions of this Constitution shall come into force on the 
twenty-sixth day of January, 1950, which day is referred to in this Constitution 
as the commencement of this Constitution. 
2[394A. Authoritative text in the Hindi language.—(1) The President 
shall cause to be published under his authority,— 
(a) the translation of this Constitution in the Hindi language, 
signed by the members of the Constituent Assembly, with such 
modifications as may be necessary to bring it in conformity with the 
language, style and terminology adopted in the authoritative texts of 
Central Acts in the Hindi language, and incorporating therein all the 
amendments of this Constitution made before such publication; and
(b) the translation in the Hindi language of every amendment of 
this Constitution made in the English language. 
(2) The translation of this Constitution and of every amendment thereof 
published under clause (1) shall be construed to have the same meaning as  the 
original thereof and if any difficulty arises in so construing any part of such 
translation, the President shall cause the same to be revised suitably.
(3) The translation of this Constitution and of every amendment thereof 
published under this article shall  be deemed to be, for all purposes, the 
authoritative text thereof in the Hindi language.]
395. Repeals.—
The Indian Independence Act, 1947, and the 
Government of India Act, 1935, together with all enactments amending or 
supplementing the latter Act, but not including the Abolition of Privy Council 
Jurisdiction Act, 1949, are hereby repealed.
______________________________________________
1. Ins. by the Constitution (Fifty-eighth Amendment) Act, 1987, s. 2 (w.e.f. 9-12-1987).
2. Art 394A, Ins. by s. 3, ibid. (w.e.f. 9-12-1987).

The partial document outlines the First Schedule of the Constitution of India, detailing the territories of various states and union territories. It specifies the territories included in each state, referencing various legislative acts that have influenced territorial boundaries over time. Key points include:

1. **State Territories**: The document lists states such as Bihar, Gujarat, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, and others, along with the specific territories that comprise each state as defined by historical acts like the States Reorganisation Act and various boundary alteration acts.

2. **Exclusions and Modifications**: It notes exclusions from certain territories based on previous legislative changes, indicating how boundaries have been altered through acts like the Bihar and Uttar Pradesh (Alteration of Boundaries) Act and the Madhya Pradesh Reorganisation Act.

3. **Union Territories**: The document also mentions union territories, including Delhi, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, and Puducherry, specifying their territories as defined by prior administrative structures.

4. **Amendments and Updates**: The text includes references to amendments and updates to the schedule, reflecting changes in territorial definitions and the establishment of new states or union territories over time.

5. **Legislative Framework**: The document serves as a legal framework for understanding the administrative divisions of India, highlighting the complexity of territorial governance and the historical context of state formation.

Overall, the document is a comprehensive enumeration of the states and union territories of India, their respective territories, and the legislative context that governs these definitions.

It specifies the monthly salaries for the President (10,000 rupees) and Governors (5,500 rupees), along with allowances that were previously applicable to the Governor-General and provincial governors before the Constitution's commencement. Additionally, it details the salaries and allowances for the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the House of the People and the Council of States, as well as for the legislative assembly and council of states, referencing the compensation that was in place prior to the Constitution.

nodes.title: Provisions as to the Judges of the Supreme Court and of the High Courts
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines provisions related to the salaries, allowances, and conditions of service for judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts in India, as specified in the Second Schedule of the Constitution. It details the salary rates for the Chief Justice and other judges, stipulating reductions in salary for those receiving pensions from previous government service. It also mentions the entitlement of judges to official residences without rent, travel allowances, and the governance of their leave and pension rights based on prior provisions applicable to the Federal Court judges. Additionally, it includes provisions for the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India, specifying their salary and conditions of service. The document further contains forms of oaths for ministers and candidates for election to Parliament, emphasizing their commitment to uphold the Constitution and maintain confidentiality in their duties.

nodes.summary: The partial document outlines the emoluments, allowances, and privileges of the President of India and the Governors of the States as specified in the Second Schedule of the Constitution. It states the monthly salaries for the President (10,000 rupees) and the Governors (5,500 rupees), and mentions that they are entitled to allowances similar to those received by their predecessors before the Constitution came into effect. Additionally, it affirms that the President and Governors will retain the same privileges as the former Governor-General and provincial Governors. It also specifies that individuals acting in these roles will receive the same emoluments and privileges as the officials they are replacing.

nodes.title: THIRD SCHEDULE
Forms of Oaths or Affirmations
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines various forms of oaths or affirmations required for different officials in India, as specified in the Third Schedule of the Constitution. It includes the oath of office for Union Ministers, State Ministers, candidates for election to Parliament and State Legislatures, members of Parliament and State Legislatures, as well as judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts. Each oath emphasizes allegiance to the Constitution of India, the commitment to uphold the sovereignty and integrity of the nation, and the duty to perform their responsibilities without bias or favoritism. Additionally, the document includes a Fourth Schedule that details the allocation of seats in the Council of States for various states and Union territories, indicating the number of seats assigned to each.

nodes.title: FIFTH SCHEDULE
Provisions as to the Administration and Control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines the provisions related to the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in India, as specified in the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution. It includes several key points:

1. **General Provisions**: Defines the term "State" in the context of Scheduled Areas, clarifying that it excludes certain northeastern states. It establishes that the executive power of a State extends to Scheduled Areas and mandates the Governor to report to the President on their administration.

2. **Tribes Advisory Council**: Each State with Scheduled Areas must establish a Tribes Advisory Council to advise on the welfare and advancement of Scheduled Tribes. The composition, appointment, and functioning of the Council are regulated by the Governor.

3. **Law Applicability**: The Governor has the authority to exempt certain Acts from applying to Scheduled Areas or modify their application. The Governor can also make regulations for governance in these areas, including land transfer restrictions and business regulations.

4. **Scheduled Areas Definition**: The document defines "Scheduled Areas" and outlines the President's powers to declare, modify, or rescind such areas, including the ability to adjust boundaries and create new Scheduled Areas.

5. **Amendment of the Schedule**: Parliament can amend the provisions of the Fifth Schedule, and such amendments are not considered constitutional amendments under Article 368.

Overall, the document emphasizes the governance framework for Scheduled Areas and the rights and protections for Scheduled Tribes, ensuring their welfare and administrative autonomy.

nodes.title: Constitution of District Councils and Regional Councils.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines provisions related to the governance of autonomous districts and regions in India as specified in the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution. Key points include:

1. **Governor's Authority**: The Governor can issue orders regarding the administration of autonomous districts after considering reports from a designated Commission.

2. **District and Regional Councils**: Each autonomous district will have a District Council with a maximum of thirty members, including elected representatives and those nominated by the Governor. Additionally, separate Regional Councils will be established for autonomous regions.

3. **Council Composition and Elections**: The document details the composition, election procedures, and qualifications for members of the District and Regional Councils, emphasizing adult suffrage and the role of the Governor in rule-making.

4. **Powers and Administration**: The District and Regional Councils are granted specific powers for local governance, including the ability to make laws on various subjects such as education, agriculture, and infrastructure, subject to the Governor's assent.

5. **Amendments and Provisions**: The text references several amendments that have modified the structure and powers of the councils, particularly in relation to specific regions like Assam.

6. **Operational Rules**: The document stipulates that the councils can create rules for their functioning, including the establishment of subordinate local councils and the conduct of business.

Overall, the document emphasizes the framework for self-governance in tribal areas, outlining the roles, powers, and responsibilities of the District and Regional Councils under the Sixth Schedule.

It outlines the powers of District Councils and Regional Councils to make laws on various subjects, including land use, agriculture, education, public health, and local governance. The document specifies the process for law-making, including the requirement for laws to be submitted to the Governor for assent and the role of the President in approving or returning laws for reconsideration. Additionally, it details the establishment of village councils or courts for administering justice among Scheduled Tribes, emphasizing the autonomy of these councils in legal matters. The text also notes amendments made to the provisions over time, reflecting changes in governance structures and responsibilities.

nodes.title: Administration of justice in autonomous districts and autonomous regions.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines provisions related to the administration of justice in autonomous districts and regions as specified in the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution of India. Key points include:

1. **Law Submission and Effect**: Any laws made under the specified provisions must be submitted to the Governor for assent before they take effect.

2. **Village Councils and Courts**: Regional and District Councils can establish village councils or courts to handle disputes among Scheduled Tribes, excluding certain cases. They have the authority to appoint members and presiding officers for these councils and courts.

3. **Court Jurisdiction**: The Regional or District Councils, or courts established by them, have appellate jurisdiction over cases tried by village councils, with the High Court and Supreme Court retaining jurisdiction over specified matters.

4. **Rule-Making Authority**: Councils may create rules regarding the constitution and powers of village councils and courts, trial procedures, and enforcement of decisions, subject to the Governor's approval.

5. **Governor's Powers**: The Governor has the authority to confer powers under the Code of Civil Procedure and the Code of Criminal Procedure to District and Regional Councils for specific cases and can modify or withdraw these powers as necessary.

6. **Exclusions from General Laws**: The general application of the Code of Civil Procedure and the Code of Criminal Procedure is limited in autonomous districts and regions, except as explicitly provided in the document. 

Overall, the document emphasizes the autonomy of local governance in legal matters for Scheduled Tribes while outlining the roles of the Governor and the councils in administering justice.

nodes.title: District and Regional Funds.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines provisions related to the governance and administrative powers of autonomous districts and regions in India as specified in the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution. Key points include:

1. **Governor's Authority**: The document specifies that the Governor cannot confer certain powers to District or Regional Councils in autonomous areas without presidential appointment.

2. **District Council Powers**: It details the powers of District Councils to establish and manage primary schools, dispensaries, markets, and other local infrastructure, with the Governor's prior approval for regulations.

3. **District and Regional Funds**: It establishes the creation of District and Regional Funds for financial management, including rules for their management, auditing, and reporting to the Governor.

4. **Revenue Collection**: The document grants Regional and District Councils the authority to assess and collect land revenue and impose taxes on lands, buildings, and various professions within their jurisdictions. 

Overall, the text emphasizes the administrative autonomy and financial governance of autonomous districts and regions in India.

nodes.summary: The partial document outlines specific territories in India as defined in the First Schedule of the Constitution. It details the territories associated with various states, including Odisha, Punjab, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, and West Bengal, along with references to historical acts that influenced their boundaries and administration. Each entry specifies the territories as they were before the Constitution's commencement, along with amendments and exclusions from previous legislative acts, such as the States Reorganisation Act and various boundary alteration acts. The document emphasizes the legal framework governing the territorial definitions and changes over time.

Additionally, it lists union territories like Delhi, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, Puducherry, and Chandigarh, specifying their historical context and the legislative acts that defined their boundaries. The document also notes amendments and renumbering of entries related to these territories over time.

263
SECOND SCHEDULE
[Articles 59(3), 65(3), 75(6), 97, 125, 148(3), 158(3), 164 (5), 186 and 221] 
PART A 
PROVISIONS AS TO THE PRESIDENT AND THE GOVERNORS OF STATES 1***
1. There shall be paid to the President and to the Governors of the States
1***  the following emoluments per mensem, that is to say:—
The President
……                10,000 rupees .
The Governor of a State     ……   
5,500 rupees .
2. There shall also be paid to the President and to the Governors of the 
States 2***  such allowances as were payable respectively to the Governor-
General of the Dominion of India and to the Governors of the corresponding 
Provinces immediately before the commencement of this Constitution.
3. The President and the Governors of 3[the States] throughout their respective 
terms of office shall be entitled to the same privileges to which the Governor-
General and the Governors of the corresponding Provinces were respectively 
entitled immediately before the commencement of this Constitution.
4. While the Vice-President or any other person  is discharging the 
functions of, or is acting as, President, or any person is discharging the 
functions of the Governor,  he shall be entitled to the same emoluments, 
allowances and privileges as the President or the Governor whose functions he 
discharges or for whom he acts, as the case may be.
4*                           *                          * 
*                         *
______________________________________________
1. The words and letter "specified in Part A of the First Schedule" omitted by the 
Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, s. 29 and Sch. (w.e.f. 1-11-1956).
Now five lakh rupees, vide the Finance Act, 2018 (13 of 2018), s. 137.
(w.e.f. 1-1-2016).
Now three lakh fifty thousand rupees, by s. 161, ibid., (w.e.f. 1-1-2016).
2. The words "so specified" omitted by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 
1956, s. 29 and Sch. (w.e.f. 1-11-1956).
3. Subs. by s. 29 and Sch., ibid., for "such states" (w.e.f. 1-11-1956).
4. Part B omitted by  s. 29 and Sch., ibid. (w.e.f. 1-11-1956).

PROVISIONS AS TO THE PRESIDENT AND THE GOVERNORS OF STATES
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines provisions related to the emoluments, allowances, and privileges of the President of India and the Governors of States, as well as the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the House of the People and the Council of States. It specifies the monthly salaries for the President (10,000 rupees) and Governors (5,500 rupees), along with allowances equivalent to those previously held by the Governor-General and provincial governors before the Constitution's commencement. It also states that individuals acting in these roles are entitled to the same benefits. Additionally, it details the salaries and allowances for the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the House of the People and the Council of States, as well as for the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of State Legislative Assemblies and their counterparts in Legislative Councils, based on previous entitlements before the Constitution was enacted.

nodes.summary: The partial document outlines provisions related to the salaries and allowances of key legislative and judicial figures in India as specified in the Constitution. It details the compensation for the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the House of the People, the Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Council of States, as well as the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Legislative Assembly and the Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Legislative Council of a State. Additionally, it addresses the salaries of the Judges of the Supreme Court, including the Chief Justice and other Judges, along with provisions for pension adjustments and the entitlement to official residences without rent. The document also notes amendments made to these provisions over time.

nodes.title: PROVISIONS AS TO THE JUDGES OF THE SUPREME COURT AND OF THE HIGH COURTS
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines provisions related to the salaries, allowances, and conditions of service for the Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts in India, as specified in the Second Schedule of the Constitution. Key points include:

1. **Salary Structure**: The document specifies the monthly salaries for the Chief Justice and other Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, with provisions for reductions in salary if the judges are receiving pensions from previous government service.

2. **Official Residence**: Judges of the Supreme Court are entitled to an official residence without rent, with certain exceptions for judges who held prior positions before the Constitution's commencement.

3. **Travel Allowances**: Judges are entitled to reasonable allowances for travel expenses incurred while on duty, as prescribed by the President.

4. **Leave and Pension Rights**: The rights regarding leave of absence and pension for Supreme Court Judges are governed by the provisions applicable to the Judges of the Federal Court prior to the Constitution's commencement.

5. **Special Pay**: Judges who were previously holding higher-paying positions before the Constitution's commencement are entitled to receive special pay to match their previous salaries.

6. **Definitions**: The document clarifies terms such as "Chief Justice," "Judge," and "actual service," detailing what constitutes time spent in service.

7. **Comptroller and Auditor-General**: Provisions for the salary and conditions of service for the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India are also included, indicating that their salary aligns with that of the Supreme Court Judges. 

Overall, the document establishes the financial and operational framework for the judiciary's leadership in India.

nodes.title: FIFTH SCHEDULE
Provisions as to the Administration and Control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines the provisions related to the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in India, as specified in the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution. It includes several key points:

1. **General Provisions**: Defines the term "State" in the context of Scheduled Areas, clarifying that it excludes certain northeastern states. It establishes that the executive power of a State extends to Scheduled Areas and mandates the Governor to report to the President on their administration.

2. **Tribes Advisory Council**: Establishes the requirement for a Tribes Advisory Council in states with Scheduled Areas, detailing its composition, duties, and the Governor's authority to regulate its functioning.

3. **Law Applicability**: Grants the Governor the power to exempt certain laws from applying to Scheduled Areas or to modify their application, as well as to create regulations for governance in these areas, particularly concerning land and business practices.

4. **Scheduled Areas Definition**: Defines "Scheduled Areas" and outlines the President's authority to declare, modify, or rescind such areas, including provisions for boundary adjustments and the creation of new Scheduled Areas.

5. **Amendment of the Schedule**: Allows Parliament to amend the provisions of the Fifth Schedule without it being considered an amendment to the Constitution under Article 368.

Overall, the document emphasizes the governance framework for Scheduled Areas and the rights and protections for Scheduled Tribes, ensuring their welfare and advancement.

It begins with general interpretations, clarifying that the term "State" excludes certain northeastern states. nodes.title: SIXTH SCHEDULE
Provisions as to the Administration of Tribal Areas in the States of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines the provisions related to the administration of tribal areas in the states of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram as per the Sixth Schedule of the Indian Constitution. Key points include:

1. **Autonomous Districts and Regions**: It establishes that tribal areas are designated as autonomous districts, with the Governor having the authority to create autonomous regions within these districts based on the presence of different Scheduled Tribes.

2. **Governor's Powers**: The Governor can modify the boundaries of autonomous districts, create new districts, and make other administrative changes, subject to certain conditions and the consideration of reports from appointed commissions.

3. **District and Regional Councils**: Each autonomous district will have a District Council, consisting of elected and nominated members, while autonomous regions will have separate Regional Councils. The councils are responsible for local governance and administration.

4. **Elections and Composition**: The document specifies the composition, election process, and term of office for members of the District and Regional Councils, including provisions for the appointment of officers and staff.

5. **Legislative Powers**: The councils have the authority to make laws on various subjects, with certain laws requiring the Governor's assent to take effect.

6. **Amendments and Provisions**: The document includes references to amendments and specific provisions applicable to different states, highlighting the evolving nature of governance in these tribal areas. 

Overall, the document emphasizes the autonomy and self-governance of tribal areas while outlining the framework for their administration and legislative powers.

nodes.summary: The partial document outlines provisions related to the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution of India, which pertains to the governance and administration of autonomous regions and districts, particularly in the northeastern states. It details the powers of District and Regional Councils to make laws on various subjects, including land use, agriculture, education, public health, and social welfare. The document specifies the process for law-making, including the requirement for laws to be submitted to the Governor for assent and the role of the President in reviewing certain laws. Additionally, it discusses the establishment of village councils or courts for administering justice within these autonomous areas, emphasizing the jurisdiction of these councils over disputes involving Scheduled Tribes. The text also notes amendments made to the provisions over time, reflecting changes in governance structures and responsibilities.

nodes.title: Administration of justice in autonomous districts and autonomous regions.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines provisions related to the administration of justice in autonomous districts and regions as specified in the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution of India. Key points include:

1. **Law Submission and Effect**: Laws made under the specified provisions must be submitted to the Governor for assent before taking effect.

2. **Village Councils and Courts**: Regional and District Councils can establish village councils or courts to handle disputes among Scheduled Tribes, excluding certain cases. They have the authority to appoint members and presiding officers for these councils and courts.

3. **Court Jurisdiction**: The Regional or District Councils have appellate jurisdiction over cases tried by village councils, with the High Court and Supreme Court retaining jurisdiction over specified matters.

4. **Rule-Making Authority**: Councils can create rules regarding the constitution and powers of village councils and courts, trial procedures, and enforcement of decisions, subject to the Governor's approval.

5. **Governor's Powers**: The Governor can confer powers under the Code of Civil Procedure and the Code of Criminal Procedure to District and Regional Councils for specific cases and may withdraw or modify these powers.

6. **Establishment of Local Institutions**: District Councils can establish and manage primary schools, dispensaries, and other local institutions, with regulations subject to the Governor's approval.

7. **Financial Provisions**: Each autonomous district and region will have designated funds to manage financial resources received by the respective councils for administration.

Overall, the document emphasizes the autonomy of local councils in governance and justice administration while outlining the oversight role of the Governor.

nodes.title: Powers of the District Council to establish primary schools, etc.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines provisions related to the governance and administrative powers of autonomous districts and regions in India as specified in the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution. Key points include:

1. **Governor's Authority**: The document specifies that the Governor cannot confer certain powers to District or Regional Councils in autonomous areas without presidential appointment.

2. **District Council Powers**: It details the powers of District Councils to establish and manage primary schools, dispensaries, markets, and other local infrastructure, with the Governor's prior approval for regulations.

3. **District and Regional Funds**: It establishes the creation of District and Regional Funds for financial management, including rules for their management, auditing, and reporting to the Governor.

4. **Revenue Collection**: The document grants Regional and District Councils the authority to assess and collect land revenue and impose taxes on lands, buildings, and various professions within their jurisdictions. 

Overall, the text emphasizes the administrative autonomy and financial governance of autonomous districts and regions in India.

nodes.title: District and Regional Funds.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines provisions related to the governance and financial management of autonomous regions and districts in India as specified in the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution. Key points include:

1. The Governor's authority to establish rules for managing District and Regional Funds, including procedures for financial transactions and custody of funds.
2. Requirements for the accounting and auditing of District and Regional Councils, with oversight by the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India.
3. The powers of Regional and District Councils to assess and collect land revenue and impose various taxes, including those on professions, animals, and market goods.
4. The ability of councils to create regulations for tax collection, which must be approved by the Governor.
5. Provisions regarding the distribution of royalties from mineral extraction, including dispute resolution by the Governor. 

Overall, the document emphasizes the financial autonomy and regulatory powers granted to local councils within autonomous regions and districts.

In case of disputes regarding royalty shares, the Governor has the authority to make a final determination. The document also notes amendments and legislative changes relevant to these provisions.

nodes.title: Licences or leases for the purpose of prospecting for, or extraction of, minerals.
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines specific provisions of the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution of India, focusing on the taxation powers of Regional and District Councils within autonomous districts. It details the types of taxes that these councils can levy, including taxes on goods entering markets, maintenance taxes for schools and roads, and entertainment taxes. Additionally, it discusses the distribution of royalties from mineral prospecting and extraction licenses, stipulating that a share of these royalties must be agreed upon between the state government and the District Council. In case of disputes regarding royalty shares, the Governor has the authority to make a final determination. The document also notes amendments and changes made to these provisions over time.

nodes.summary: The partial document outlines provisions related to the administration of tribal areas in the states of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram as specified in the Sixth Schedule of the Indian Constitution. It discusses the establishment of autonomous districts and regions within these tribal areas, detailing the Governor's authority to create, modify, or reorganize these districts and regions. Key points include the ability to divide areas inhabited by different Scheduled Tribes into autonomous regions, include or exclude areas from designated parts of the schedule, create new autonomous districts, and alter the boundaries and names of existing districts. The document also notes amendments and provisions specific to certain areas, such as the Bodoland Territorial Areas District.

each autonomous district, a District Fund and for each autonomous region, a 
Regional Fund to which shall be credited all moneys received respectively

case may be, in accordance with the provisions of this Constitution.

lands within such region and the District Council for an autonomous district 
in respect of all lands within the district except those which are in the areas 
under the authority of Regional Councils, if any, within the district, shall 
have the power to assess and collect revenue in respect of such lands in 
accordance with the principles for the time being followed 2[by the 
Government of the State in assessing lands for the purpose of land revenue 
in the State generally.]

within such region and the District Council for an autonomous district in 
respect of all areas in the district except those which are under the authority of 
Regional Councils, if any, within the district, shall have power to levy and 
collect taxes on lands and buildings, and tolls on persons resident within such 
areas.

The Second Schedule addresses the emoluments, allowances, and privileges of the President, Governors, Speakers, and Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, specifying their salaries and conditions of service. It highlights the financial provisions for these officials, including adjustments for those receiving pensions from previous service. Overall, the document serves as a legal reference for the administrative structure and compensation of key governmental roles in India.

(iii) joining time on transfer from a High Court to the Supreme 
Court or from one High Court to another. 
PART E
PROVISIONS AS TO THE COMPTROLLER AND AUDITOR-GENERAL OF INDIA 
12. (1) There shall be paid to the Comptroller and Auditor-General of 
India a salary at the rate of *four thousand rupees per mensem.
(2) The person who was holding office immediately before the 
commencement of this Constitution as Auditor-General of India and has 
become on such commencement the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India 
under article 377 shall in addition to the salary specified in sub-paragraph (1) of 
this paragraph be entitled to receive as special pay an amount equivalent to the 
difference between the salary so specified and the salary which he was drawing 
as Auditor-General of India immediately before such commencement.
(3) The rights in respect of leave of absence and pension and the other 
conditions of service of the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India shall be 
governed or shall continue to be governed, as the case may be, by the provisions 
which were applicable to the Auditor-General of India immediately before the 
commencement of this Constitution and all references in those provisions to the 
Governor-General shall be construed as references to the President.
______________________________________________
* The Comptroller and Auditor-General of India shall be paid a salary equal to 
the salary of the Judges of the Supreme Court vide s. 3 of the Comptroller and 
Auditor-General (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 (56 of 
1971) .  The salary of Judges of the Supreme Court has been raised to two 
lakh fifty thousand rupees per mensem by the High Court and Supreme Court 
Judges (Salaries and Conditions of Service) Amendment Act, 2018 (10 of 2018), s. 6 
(w.e.f. 1-1-2016).

It details the compensation for the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the House of the People, the Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Council of States, as well as the Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Legislative Assembly and the Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Legislative Council of a State. Additionally, it includes provisions for the salaries of Judges of the Supreme Court, detailing specific salary rates for the Chief Justice and other Judges, along with conditions regarding pension adjustments and the provision of official residences for Judges. The text also notes amendments made to these provisions over time.

nodes.title: FIFTH SCHEDULE
Provisions as to the Administration and Control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines the provisions related to the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in India, as specified in the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution. It includes several key points:

1. **Interpretation and Scope**: Defines "State" in the context of Scheduled Areas, excluding certain northeastern states.

2. **Executive Power**: States that the executive power of a State extends to Scheduled Areas, with the Governor required to report to the President on their administration.

3. **Tribes Advisory Council**: Establishes the requirement for a Tribes Advisory Council in states with Scheduled Areas, detailing its composition, duties, and the Governor's authority to regulate its functioning.

4. **Law Applicability**: Grants the Governor the power to exempt certain laws from applying to Scheduled Areas and to make regulations for governance, including land transfer and business practices among Scheduled Tribes.

5. **Scheduled Areas Definition**: Defines Scheduled Areas and outlines the President's authority to declare, modify, or rescind such areas.

6. **Amendment of the Schedule**: Allows Parliament to amend the provisions of the Schedule without it being considered a constitutional amendment.

Overall, the document emphasizes the governance framework for Scheduled Areas and the rights and protections for Scheduled Tribes, ensuring their welfare and advancement.

Provisions as to the Administration and Control of Scheduled Areas and

PART A 
GENERAL
1. Interpretation.—In this Schedule, unless the context otherwise 
requires, the expression “State” 1*** does not include the 2[States of Assam
3[, 4[Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.]]]
2. Executive power of a State in Scheduled Areas.—Subject to the 
provisions of this Schedule, the executive power of a State extends to the 
Scheduled Areas therein.

administration of Scheduled Areas.—The  Governor 5*** of each State having 
Scheduled Areas therein shall annually, or whenever so required by the President, 
make a report to the President regarding the administration of the Scheduled 
Areas in that State and the executive power of the Union shall extend to the 
giving of directions to the State as to the administration of the said areas.

ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL OF SCHEDULED AREAS AND 
SCHEDULED TRIBES
4. Tribes Advisory Council.—(1) There shall be established in each 
State having Scheduled Areas therein and, if the President so directs, also in 
any State having Scheduled Tribes but not Scheduled Areas therein, a Tribes 
Advisory Council consisting of not more than twenty members of whom, as 
nearly as may be, three-fourths shall be the representatives of the Scheduled 
Tribes in the Legislative Assembly of the State:

nodes.title: SIXTH SCHEDULE
Provisions as to the Administration of Tribal Areas
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines provisions related to the administration of tribal areas in the states of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram as per the Sixth Schedule of the Indian Constitution. Key points include:

1. **Autonomous Districts and Regions**: It establishes that tribal areas are designated as autonomous districts, with the Governor having the authority to create autonomous regions within these districts based on the presence of different Scheduled Tribes.

2. **Governor's Powers**: The Governor can modify the boundaries of autonomous districts, create new districts, and make other administrative changes, subject to the consideration of reports from appointed commissions.

3. **District and Regional Councils**: Each autonomous district will have a District Council, consisting of elected and nominated members, while autonomous regions will have separate Regional Councils. The councils are corporate bodies with defined powers and responsibilities for local governance.

4. **Elections and Composition**: The document specifies the composition, election process, and term of office for members of the District and Regional Councils, including provisions for the appointment of officers and staff.

5. **Legislative Powers**: The councils have the authority to make laws on various subjects, with certain laws requiring the Governor's assent to take effect.

6. **Amendments and Provisions**: The text includes references to amendments and specific provisions applicable to certain districts, such as the Bodoland Territorial Council and the North Cachar Hills Autonomous Council, highlighting the evolving nature of governance in these regions.

It details the powers of District and Regional Councils to make laws on various subjects, including land use, agriculture, education, public health, and social welfare. The document specifies the process for law-making, including the requirement for laws to be submitted to the Governor for assent and the President's role in reviewing certain laws. Additionally, it discusses the establishment of village councils or courts for administering justice among Scheduled Tribes, emphasizing their jurisdiction and the limitations on other courts. The text also notes amendments made to the provisions over time, reflecting changes in governance structures and responsibilities.

nodes.title: Administration of justice in autonomous districts and autonomous regions.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines provisions related to the administration of justice and governance in autonomous districts and regions under the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution of India. Key points include:

1. **Law Submission and Effect**: Laws made by councils must be submitted to the Governor for assent before taking effect.

2. **Judicial Authority**: Regional and District Councils can establish village councils or courts to handle disputes among Scheduled Tribes, with limited jurisdiction for appeals, primarily to the High Court and Supreme Court.

3. **Rule-Making Powers**: Councils can create rules for the functioning of village councils and courts, including procedures for trials and appeals.

4. **Governor's Powers**: The Governor has the authority to confer powers under civil and criminal procedure codes to councils for specific cases and can withdraw these powers.

5. **Local Governance**: District Councils can establish and manage local services such as schools and health facilities, with the Governor's approval for regulations.

6. **Financial Management**: Establishment of District and Regional Funds for managing finances, including auditing by the Comptroller and Auditor-General.

7. **Taxation Powers**: Councils have the authority to assess and collect land revenue and impose various taxes within their jurisdictions.

8. **Mineral Royalties**: Provisions for sharing royalties from mineral extraction with District Councils, with disputes referred to the Governor.

9. **Regulation of Non-Tribal Activities**: District Councils can regulate money-lending and trading by non-tribals, including licensing and interest rate controls.

Overall, the document emphasizes the autonomy of local councils in governance, justice administration, and financial management within specified regions.

nodes.title: Power of District Council to make regulations for the control of money-lending and trading by non-tribals.
nodes.summary: The partial document outlines provisions related to the regulation of money-lending and trading by non-tribals in autonomous districts of India, as specified in the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution. It grants the District Council the authority to create regulations governing these activities, including licensing requirements for money-lenders and traders, setting maximum interest rates, and maintaining account records. The document also mentions amendments to these provisions, particularly concerning the states of Tripura, Mizoram, and Assam, and emphasizes that regulations must be approved by a majority of the District Council and the Governor before taking effect. Additionally, it states that all laws and regulations made under this Schedule must be published in the Official Gazette to have legal force.

nodes.summary: The partial document outlines provisions related to the governance of autonomous districts and regions in the states of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram under the Sixth Schedule of the Indian Constitution. It details the legislative powers of District and Regional Councils, including their authority to make laws concerning specific matters, and the conditions under which state and parliamentary laws may apply or be modified in these autonomous areas. The document also discusses the role of the Governor and the President in directing the applicability of laws, including the possibility of retrospective effects. Additionally, it addresses the financial management of autonomous districts, requiring that their estimated receipts and expenditures be presented separately in the state's annual financial statement. Lastly, it mentions the appointment of a Commission by the Governor to investigate and report on the administration of these autonomous regions, focusing on various aspects such as education, healthcare, and the need for special legislation.

nodes.summary: The partial document outlines provisions related to the administration of tribal areas in the states of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram as specified in the Sixth Schedule of the Indian Constitution. It discusses the establishment of autonomous districts and regions within these tribal areas, detailing the Governor's authority to create, modify, or reorganize these districts and regions. Key points include the ability to divide areas inhabited by different Scheduled Tribes into autonomous regions, include or exclude areas from designated parts of the schedule, create new autonomous districts, and alter the boundaries and names of existing districts. The document also notes amendments and provisions specific to certain areas, such as the Bodoland Territorial Areas District.

nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines specific provisions from the Constitution of India, focusing on the First and Second Schedules. The First Schedule lists the names and territories of various states and union territories, detailing their formation through reorganization acts, such as the Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Andhra Pradesh, and Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Acts. It includes territories like Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand, Jharkhand, Telangana, Delhi, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep, Dadra and Nagar Haveli, Daman and Diu, Puducherry, Chandigarh, Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh.

The Second Schedule addresses the emoluments and privileges of key constitutional positions, including the President, Governors of States, Speakers of legislative bodies, and Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts. It specifies their salaries, allowances, and conditions of service, including provisions for those who were previously in office before the Constitution's commencement. The document also includes forms of oaths or affirmations for ministers and candidates for election to Parliament.

Additionally, it details the salaries and allowances for the legislative leaders, ensuring they align with those of their predecessors in the Dominion of India. The document includes references to amendments and changes made to the original provisions.

nodes.title: PART D PROVISIONS AS TO THE JUDGES OF THE SUPREME COURT AND OF THE HIGH COURTS
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines provisions related to the salaries, allowances, and conditions of service for the Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts in India, as specified in the Second Schedule of the Constitution. Key points include:

1. **Salary Structure**: The document specifies the monthly salaries for the Chief Justice and other Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, with provisions for reductions in salary if the judges are receiving pensions from previous government service.

2. **Official Residence**: Judges of the Supreme Court are entitled to an official residence without rent, with certain exceptions for judges who held prior positions before the Constitution's commencement.

3. **Travel Allowances**: Judges are entitled to reasonable allowances for travel expenses incurred while on duty, as prescribed by the President.

4. **Leave and Pension Rights**: The rights regarding leave of absence and pension for Supreme Court Judges are governed by the provisions applicable to the Judges of the Federal Court prior to the Constitution's commencement.

5. **Special Pay**: Judges who were previously holding higher salaries before the Constitution's commencement are entitled to receive special pay to match their previous earnings.

6. **Definitions**: The document clarifies terms such as "Chief Justice," "Judge," and "actual service," detailing what constitutes time spent in service.

7. **Comptroller and Auditor-General**: Provisions for the salary and conditions of service for the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India are also included, indicating a salary structure and rights similar to those of the Judges of the Supreme Court. 

Overall, the document establishes the financial and operational framework for the judiciary's top officials in India.

nodes.summary: The partial document outlines the oaths or affirmations required for various public officials in India, specifically candidates for the Council of States and the House of the People, as well as judges of the Supreme Court and the Comptroller and Auditor-General. Each oath emphasizes a commitment to uphold the Constitution of India, maintain the sovereignty and integrity of the nation, and faithfully perform their duties. The text also notes an amendment related to the oaths, indicating a formal legal framework for these affirmations.

“I, A.B., having been nominated as a  candidate  to  fill  a  seat in the

solemnly affirm
that I will bear true  faith and allegiance to the Constitution of India as 
by law established and that I will uphold the sovereignty and integrity of 
India.” 
B

“I,  A.B., having been elected  (or  nominated)  a member of  the 
Council  of  States  (or  the House of  the People) do swear in  the name of  God   
                                                                                   solemnly affirm
that I will bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution of India as by 
law established, that I will uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India 
and that I will faithfully discharge the duty upon which I am about to 
enter.”]
IV
Form of oath or affirmation to be made by the Judges of the Supreme 
Court and the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India:—
“I, A.B., having been appointed Chief Justice (or a Judge) of  the 
Supreme Court of  India  (or Comptroller and Auditor-General  of  
India)  do  swear  in  the  name  of   God that I  will  bear  true  faith and
solemnly affirm
faith and allegiance to the Constitution of India as by law established, 
1[that I will uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India,] that I will 
duly and faithfully and to the best of my ability, knowledge and 
judgment perform the duties of my office without fear or favour,

nodes.title: FIFTH SCHEDULE
Provisions as to the Administration and Control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines the provisions related to the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in India, as specified in the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution. It includes several key points:

1. **Interpretation and Scope**: Defines "State" in the context of Scheduled Areas, excluding certain northeastern states.

2. **Executive Power**: States that the executive power of a State extends to Scheduled Areas, with the Governor required to report to the President on their administration.

3. **Tribes Advisory Council**: Establishes the requirement for a Tribes Advisory Council in states with Scheduled Areas, detailing its composition, duties, and the Governor's authority to regulate its functioning.

4. **Law Applicability**: Grants the Governor the power to exempt certain laws from applying to Scheduled Areas and to make regulations for governance, including land transfer and business practices among Scheduled Tribes.

5. **Scheduled Areas Definition**: Defines Scheduled Areas and outlines the President's authority to declare, modify, or rescind such areas.

6. **Amendment of the Schedule**: Allows Parliament to amend the provisions of the Schedule without it being considered a constitutional amendment.

Overall, the document emphasizes the governance framework for Scheduled Areas and the rights and protections for Scheduled Tribes within those regions.

Administration of justice in autonomous districts and autonomous regions.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines provisions related to the administration of justice in autonomous districts and regions as specified in the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution of India. Key points include:

1. **Law Submission and Effect**: Laws made under the specified provisions must be submitted to the Governor for assent before taking effect.

2. **Village Councils and Courts**: Regional and District Councils can establish village councils or courts to handle disputes among Scheduled Tribes, excluding certain cases. They have the authority to appoint members and presiding officers for these councils and courts.

3. **Court Jurisdiction**: The Regional or District Councils have appellate jurisdiction over cases tried by village councils, with the High Court and Supreme Court retaining jurisdiction over specified matters.

4. **Rule-Making Authority**: Councils can create rules regarding the constitution and powers of village councils and courts, trial procedures, and enforcement of decisions, subject to the Governor's approval.

5. **Governor's Powers**: The Governor can confer powers under the Code of Civil Procedure and the Code of Criminal Procedure to District and Regional Councils for specific cases and may withdraw or modify these powers.

6. **Establishment of Local Institutions**: District Councils can establish and manage primary schools, dispensaries, and other local institutions, with regulations subject to the Governor's approval.

7. **Financial Provisions**: Each autonomous district and region will have designated funds to manage financial resources received by the respective councils for administration.

Overall, the document emphasizes the autonomy of local councils in governance and justice administration while outlining the oversight role of the Governor.

nodes.title: Powers of the District Council to establish primary schools, etc.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines provisions related to the governance and administrative powers of District and Regional Councils in autonomous districts and regions as per the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution of India. Key points include:

1. **Authority of the Governor**: The document specifies limitations on the Governor's powers concerning the District and Regional Councils, particularly in relation to the establishment of autonomous districts and regions.

2. **Powers of District Councils**: It details the powers granted to District Councils to establish and manage primary schools, dispensaries, markets, and other local infrastructure, with the requirement of prior approval from the Governor for certain regulations.

3. **Financial Management**: The establishment of District and Regional Funds is mandated, which will hold all financial resources received by the respective councils. The Governor is given the authority to make rules regarding the management of these funds, including auditing procedures.

4. **Taxation Powers**: The document outlines the taxation powers of the District and Regional Councils, allowing them to assess and collect land revenue, impose taxes on various activities, and levy tolls, with regulations needing the Governor's assent.

5. **Royalties from Mineral Extraction**: It addresses the distribution of royalties from mineral extraction licenses, stipulating that a share of these royalties will be allocated to the District Councils, with disputes over amounts to be resolved by the Governor.

Overall, the document emphasizes the autonomy of local councils in governance while maintaining oversight by the Governor.

nodes.title: District and Regional Funds.
nodes.summary:
The partial document discusses provisions related to the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution of India, which pertains to the governance of autonomous districts and regions. Key points include:

1. **Taxation Powers**: It outlines the types of taxes that Regional and District Councils can levy, such as taxes on goods entering markets, maintenance of public services, and entertainment taxes. Regulations for the collection of these taxes must be submitted to the Governor for assent.

2. **Mineral Royalties**: The document specifies that a share of royalties from mineral extraction licenses granted by the state government must be allocated to the respective District Councils, with disputes over these shares being resolved by the Governor.

3. **Regulation of Money-Lending and Trading**: District Councils are empowered to regulate money-lending and trading activities by non-tribals, including licensing requirements and interest rate caps. Regulations require a three-fourths majority for passage and must also be submitted to the Governor.

4. **Publication of Laws**: Any laws or regulations made by the District or Regional Councils must be published in the Official Gazette to have legal force.

5. **Application of State and Parliamentary Laws**: The document details how laws from the State Legislature or Parliament apply to autonomous districts, allowing District Councils to direct the applicability of certain laws and providing the Governor with the authority to exempt specific laws from applying to these regions.

6. **Amendments and Provisions**: It notes various amendments to the provisions, indicating changes in the application of laws to specific states like Assam, Meghalaya, and Tripura, and the conditions under which these laws may be modified or exempted.

It grants the District Council the authority to create regulations governing these activities, including licensing requirements for money-lenders and traders, maximum interest rates, and the maintenance and inspection of financial records. The document also notes that regulations must be approved by a three-fourths majority of the District Council and must receive assent from the Governor to take effect. Additionally, it discusses the publication of laws and regulations in the Official Gazette, ensuring they have the force of law upon publication. Amendments to these provisions, particularly concerning their application to specific states like Tripura, Mizoram, and Assam, are also mentioned, indicating changes in the regulatory framework over time.

nodes.title: Publication of laws, rules and regulations made under the Schedule.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines provisions related to the governance and administration of autonomous districts and regions in India, specifically under the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution. Key points include:

1. **Regulation Making**: District Councils can make regulations, which require a three-fourths majority for approval and must be submitted to the Governor for assent before taking effect.

2. **Publication of Laws**: All laws and regulations made by District or Regional Councils must be published in the Official Gazette to have legal force.

3. **Application of State and Parliamentary Acts**: Specific provisions detail how Acts of the State Legislature and Parliament apply to autonomous districts, allowing for exceptions and modifications as directed by the District Council or the Governor.

4. **Financial Management**: Estimated receipts and expenditures for autonomous districts must be discussed by the District Council and presented separately in the State's annual financial statement.

5. **Commission for Administration Review**: The Governor can appoint a Commission to report on the administration of autonomous districts, focusing on education, medical facilities, and legislative needs.

6. **Governor's Powers**: The Governor has the authority to annul or suspend acts of District or Regional Councils if they threaten public safety, and can dissolve councils based on recommendations from a Commission.

7. **Elections and Constituencies**: The Governor can exclude areas from autonomous districts when forming constituencies for legislative assembly elections.

Overall, the document emphasizes the autonomy of local councils while outlining the oversight and regulatory powers of the Governor and the State Legislature.

nodes.title: Application of Acts of Parliament and of the Legislature of the State of Meghalaya to autonomous districts and autonomous regions in the State of Meghalaya.
nodes.summary: The partial document discusses the provisions of the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution of India, specifically focusing on the application of laws made by the District and Regional Councils in the autonomous districts and regions of Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram. It outlines the hierarchy of laws, stating that if there is a conflict between local laws and state laws, the state laws will prevail. It also details the powers of the President and Governors to exempt certain Acts of Parliament or state legislation from applying to these autonomous areas or to modify their application. The document emphasizes the autonomy of local councils in legislating on specified matters, particularly concerning the regulation of non-distilled alcoholic liquor.

Additionally, it mandates that financial estimates related to autonomous districts be presented separately in the state's annual financial statement and allows the Governor to appoint a Commission to investigate and report on various administrative matters, including educational and medical facilities, the need for new legislation, and the administration of local laws.
